title: Defense giant Saab sees orders triple after Gripen fighter jet deal with Ukraine
content:
Swedish defense giantSaabreported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine.

New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.

Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor.

The results come asEuropean governments raceto turn defense spending pledges into military capability.

Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030.

"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement.

Orders booked in the quarter also include a10.1 billion kronor orderfor its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order for systems for German frigates.

Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

Even with anever-growing order book, booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.

title: SpaceX records $561 million investment gain from stake in Elon Musk's Boring Co.
content:
SpaceX said on Thursday that its stake inElon Musk'sThe Boring Co. netted the company an investment gain of $561 million during the third quarter.

The gain accounted for more than half of SpaceX's "other income" in the period and boosted its net income, which landed at just over $4 billion, the company said in its quarterlyfinancial filingwith the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Created inside SpaceX in 2017 and spun out a year later, Boring Co. says its mission is to "revolutionize transportation" by creating underground tunnels with stations where passengers can board and exit. Last month, Boring Co.raised$3 billion at a $23 billion valuation, with backing from the United Arab Emirates and a roster of other longtime Musk supporters.

Boring Co. has announced about a dozen city projects, but its only tunnels currently open for public use are in Las Vegas, where passengers can travel in Tesla vehicles between the downtown convention center and various casino resorts using its Las Vegas Convention Center Loop.

In July of last year, Boring Co.strucka deal to build about 20 miles of tunnels in Nashville, Tennessee. The Music City Loop, as it's known, is being designed to carry paying passengers between downtown and the airport inTeslavehicles. The fast-tracked projectsparkeda partisan feud when it was greenlit and has drawn new safety concerns oversinkholerisks this week.

In the UAE, Boring Co. plans to build over 150 kilometers (93 miles) of tunnels, includinga project announcedin February of last year, the Dubai Loop.

SpaceX also said in Thursday's filing that it purchased $151 million worth ofTesla'sMegapack energy storage systems during the quarter. Musk said on SpaceX'searnings callon Tuesday that he thinks it would be a "good idea" for the two companies to merge, and said they've both created special committees to discuss a potential transaction.

title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace
content:
Etsysaid Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform.

Ina blog post, Etsy said it's banning the sale of "functional guides" that are created using AI, including patterns, cooking recipes and instructions. The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns. Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said.

Sellers will also be required to show an actual item made using the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, "so buyers know what to expect," Etsy said.

Etsysaidin a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform.

"Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote. "It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items."

As part of the move, Etsy said it's barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling.

Etsy told sellers it will continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform as long as merchants "play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process."

"Sellers must still disclose when an item is created using AI and cannot misrepresent AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own creation," the company added.

Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods. The company has beenleaning moreinto that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition fromAmazonandWalmart, as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein.

Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces. Etsy has in recent years struggled to curb the proliferation of AI-madecrochet patternsand otherAI "slop."Amazon recentlyrequired sellersto label photos or videos that feature AI-generated people in response to recent legislation mandating the disclosure.

While Etsy has cracked down on the use of AI in listings, it's been infusing the technology throughout more of its website. The company has used AI to build more detailed profiles of shoppers and surface relevant products in search results.

Etsy has also partnered withOpenAIon shopping features, including launching a ChatGPT app for product discovery.

title: Trump invokes Cold War era Defense Production Act for oil production, refining
content:
President Donald Trump determined on Thursday that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense, a move that could open up U.S. funding for fossil fuel projects.

In a presidential memo, Trump also invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, allowing him to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and storage of liquid fuels.

Prices for crude oil and diesel have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in joint action at the end of February. Since then, the conflict has limited energy shipments globally, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries exacerbating the fuel shortages.

The surge in costs poses a risk for Trump in the Nov. 3 elections, as his fellow Republicans try to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. The Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that closed Monday shows just 36% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the economy.

The memo said that without taking the actions, the U.S. is not able to provide enough of those energy services in a "timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations."

The memo did not mention specific projects that could be funded. The U.S. averaged around 13.6 million barrels of daily crude production in 2025, making it the largest crude producer worldwide.

Last ‌week, Vice President JD Vance said the administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity of a Texas refinery owned byDelek U.S. Holdings.

Trump signed legislation last year that included $1 billion in Defense Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.

title: Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
content:
The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox.

Subscribe here to get access today.

Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house fromfeuding among executives. Sometimes they come in court, frombattling the Federal Communications Commission.

And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates.

ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private.

Disney has the broadcast rights to this season'sSuper Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006.Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recentmedia rights dealwith the NFLin 2021.

The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna.

Fox saidlast yearthat Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million.

Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally.

An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers.

About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter.

Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming.

There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and chargethemretrans fees.

This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee.

For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past.

Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game.

Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI.

Disney is also airing so-called"alt-casts" of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats").

Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"-themed alt-caston Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+.

The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free.

Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.

"The Super Bowl is the year's most-watched telecast, and our broad distribution across ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ will give fans everywhere more ways than ever to enjoy the game," according to a statement provided by a Disney spokesperson. "Making marquee live events available via streaming is a well-established industry practice. Fox and NBC have recently offered the Super Bowl on Tubi and Peacock, and we've similarly streamed 'The Oscars' on Hulu and 'Dancing with the Stars' on Disney+, for example. There's nothing unprecedented about this approach as we are meeting the modern consumer where they are."

Still, the totality of it all will certainly lower broadcast viewership. One station group CEO estimated local advertising revenue associated with the game may fall 35%. That executive declined to be named because the analysis is private.

"Any time you fragment distribution, you're destroying value for each of the individual platforms," a station group CEO told me, who asked not to be named for fear of potential retribution. "I don't have a problem with what Disney is doing — I have a problem that there's no acknowledgement that we're losing money."

This issue of lower broadcast Super Bowl viewership, and associated advertising revenue, is of so much concern that it's currently being discussed at the affiliate board — an elected body of executives across the TV broadcasting industry who act as liaisons between local stations and their parent network (Disney/ABC, in this case).

It's unclear exactly how affiliates may be compensated, if at all.

The decline in traditional TV viewership is pushing Disney to broaden its coverage to new platforms and new audiences that don't watch cable or broadcast TV.

Station executives want Disney to lean in to what continues to be a profitable, albeit declining, business. Several of those executives told me privately they think Disney is doing itself and the broader linear TV ecosystem a disservice by not banding together with affiliates to keep viewers on broadcast platforms.

"Our ABC affiliates are important partners and we always take that into careful consideration when making these decisions," said a Disney spokesperson. "We've successfully navigated similar situations in collaboration with the governing board many times before, and this is no different."

The chairman of the ABC Television Affiliates Association Board of Governors declined to comment.

title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors
content:
OpenAIis closing in on a funding round that could value theartificial intelligencegiant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potentialinitial public offering.

The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.

Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.

OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round afterinvestors approached the companywith proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.

Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.

The companyconfidentially filedits prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friartold employeesin August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEOSam Altmansaidthat "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."

Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The companyconfidentially filedits prospectus with regulators in June and is activelyengaging in meetingswith prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.

In May, Anthropic closed a$65 billionfunding round at a $965 billion valuation.

title: Nasdaq falls more than 2% for worst day since June as AI spending woes, oil prices spark sell-off: Live updates
content:
Stocks mostly slid Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence companies, while oil prices jumped amid rising geopolitical tensions.

TheNasdaq Compositepulled back 2.6% to 26,008.86, while theS&P 500shed 1.21% to close at 7,663.43. The tech-heavy index suffered its worst session since June, while the S&P 500 posted its worst daily performance since July. TheDow Jones Industrial Averageinched up 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to end at 52,867.98.

Meta Platformsslipped about 7%, even as itexceeded revenue expectationsand offered upbeat guidance. Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted.Advanced Micro Devicesfell more than 8%, whileMicron TechnologyandNvidiadropped 6% and 4%, respectively.

Neocloud leaderCoreWeave, whose bond yields and credit default swapsremained elevated, declined 10% as well. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangtold CNBCThursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.

Huang's commentary about a scarcity of capital is "spooking markets and reigniting the concerns around the capital markets on the credit side being full from a risk appetite standpoint," said Wells Fargo traders in a note. They also said Meta's comments about the large amount of AI funding needed caused the shares to roll over and weighed on the overall market.

JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."

Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.

Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. PresidentDonald Trumpalso told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."

International benchmarkBrent crude futuresrose 4% to settle at $113.17 per barrel.West Texas Intermediate crude futuresadvanced 2.39% to $99.47 per barrel.

Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark10-year Treasurynote yield dropped more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, falling to itslowest level in almost a month. The2-yearnote yield also shed more than 16 basis points to 4.659%.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite saw sizable declines on Thursday.

The broad market index moved down 1.21% to 7,663.43, while the tech-heavy index decreased 2.6% to 26,008.86.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, traded just above the flatline, rising 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to 52,867.98.

Shares of power and energy companies tied to the AI boom plunged Thursday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the soaring costs of data center expansion.

Two major energy equipment players,GE VernovaandBloom Energy, led the declines, with each falling more than 11%. As investors sold their AI infrastructure stocks,Vistraalso shed over 10%, whileQuanta Servicesdropped more than 8%.Talen EnergyandEatondeclined 8.3% and nearly 7%, respectively.

The selloff came asMeta's latest earningsreport reignited concerns over AI infrastructure spending. The tech giant raised its capital expenditure forecast, highlighting the enormous investment required to support its AI ambitions and raising questions about how quickly those investments will generate returns.

Nuclear energy stocks were also caught in the downturn, withOklofalling more than 4% andNuScale Powerdeclining over 3%. The broad retreat shows a deeper, growing investor unease over whether the pace of AI infrastructure investment is sustainable.

Oil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.

Brent crudefutures gained 4% to close at $113.17 per barrel, the highest level for the international benchmark since May 4. U.S.West Texas Intermediategained 2.4% to settle at $99.47.

Modernashares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on itsclosely watched cancer vaccinedeveloped withMerck.

The stock fell even though the full data, released later Thursday following the leak, appeared positive relative to Wall Street expectations. The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.Read more.

— Annika Kim Constantino and Jacob Pramuk

Shares of Skydance fell around 1% in afternoon trading afterTeslaCEO Elon Musk made aroughly $1 billion investmentin the company.

The investment comes amid a wider effort by Skydance to raise equity investments as it looks to cut costs.

— Sarah Whitten and Sean Conlon

Check out some of the companies making the biggest moves midday:

Wolfe Research downgradedNetflixto peer perform from outperform.

Wolfe cited stagnant viewer engagement, intensifying streaming competition and concerns about the company's long-term growth prospects.

"Engagement failed to respond to rising investment, and last week's content leadership changes convince us that solutions require patience & lower incremental margins. Attention economy competition is rampant. Consensus estimates look fair. Downgrade to Peer Perform," Wolfe's analyst Peter Supino said.

The streaming giant has struggled, Supino said, to generate new hits despite increasing content spending by $3 billion over the past two years. The firm also removed its $95 price target.

Despite $3B of content expense growth over the last two years, "Netflix has lost its mojo" according to Supino. The analyst pointed to growing competition from YouTube and rival streaming platforms, adding  that higher programming costs may weigh on Netflix's future profit margins. Recent changes to Netflix's content leadership could help, but improvements will likely take time.

"In a not unreasonable downside scenario where Netflix revenue decelerates to MSD by 2030 (not our base case), we think NFLX would be worth ~$50/shr. today, and therefore do not think LT engagement / growth concerns are fully priced in," Supino said.

Shares ofCME Groupadvanced 3% on the back of an upgrade by JPMorgan.

The bank re-rated the stock to overweight from underweight and increased its December 2027 price target on the stock to $367, up from their prior $250.

JPMorgan analyst Kenneth Worthington describer the current interest rate environment as "constructive" for further growth in CME's interest rate business since the company benefits when CME activity when longer term rates are rising.

He also favors CME's launch of a series of new products, which could "evolve into larger opportunities," citing its successful launch of its crypto futures service.

The analyst also cites CME's expansion in some cases to 24/7 trading for pre-existing retail-sized contracts.

Rollinsreported weaker-than-expectedthird-quarter results as the pest control company continued to face challenges attracting residential customers.

Revenue rose 6.2% from a year earlier to $1.09 billion, while adjusted earnings came in at 33 cents per share. Analysts polled by FactSet expected a profit of 34 cents per share on revenue of $1.11 billion.

"We are disappointed with our third quarter performance and are acting with urgency to address the challenges impacting our results. We now have a clearer understanding of how the customer acquisition landscape is evolving and are taking concrete steps to optimize our approach," said President and CEO Jerry Gahlhoff Jr.

To be sure, the stock rose more than 4%.

TheDow Jones Industrial Averagelost 218 points, or 0.4%. TheS&P 500shed 0.9%, and theNasdaq Compositepulled back 1.5%.

Shares ofLockheed Martinrose more than 4% after the companyreported better-than-expected resultsfor the third quarter. Driven by strong demand for fighter jets and missile defense systems, Lockheed also hiked its earnings and revenue guidance for 2026.

The company now expects 2026 ⁠sales of about $80 billion to $82 billion, up from its previous outlook of $79.75 billion to $81.75 billion.

Sales for the defense contractor touched $20.6 billion, an increase of 11% from a year earlier. Lockheed's order backlog jumped to a record $292 billion, boosted by a $52.5 billion multiyear contract for PAC-3 missile interceptors amid heightened global defense demand.

Shares ofProcter & Gambleadded around 3% in premarket trading after the consumer goods company posted a beat on both the top and bottom lines for its fiscal first quarter..

The Tide and Pampers parent saw adjusted earnings of $2 per share, topping the $1.88 consensus estimate, according to LSEG. Revenue came in at $23.28 billion, above the $22.80 billion expected from analysts.

Procter & Gamble also raised its full-year revenue guidance to a range of 2% and 4%, up from its prior guidance of 1% to 3%.

"While we expect there will continue to be geopolitical and economic challenges, this strong start keeps us on track to deliver within our guidance ranges for organic sales growth, core EPS growth and free cash flow productivity

title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
content:
PresidentDonald Trumpon Thursday defended a controversialad by the campaignofVivek Ramaswamyfeaturing the estranged mother ofAmy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar.

Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather,Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur.

In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life."

"Don't vote for people who lie," Arthursays in the ad. "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."

Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.

Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse."

"The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."

Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him.

"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.

Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing."

"I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.

Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.

Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.

But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."

"The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."

Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.

Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.

Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do."

"My mother is not well," Acton said.

Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested.

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down.

"The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."

— CNBC'sLuke Fountaincontributed to this article.

title: 10-year Treasury yield tumbles below 5% to lowest level in nearly a month
content:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.

The benchmark10-year U.S. Treasuryyield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.

The yield on the2-year Treasury note, which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated30-year U.S. Treasury— most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."

Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.

"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."

The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangtold CNBCThursday that while demand for neoclouds is "off the charts," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are aspecialized cloud computing providersthat focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.

This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached theirhighest levels in more than two decadesamid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.

Above 5%, however,attitudes began to shiftand yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.

Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday.Oil pricesmoved sharply higher, withWest Texas Intermediatefutures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel.Brent crudefutures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.

Higher energy prices followed aNew York Times report,citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."

"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."

— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.

title: SpaceX and Tesla have high election stakes as Elon Musk pours $366 million into campaigns
content:
Elon Musk'sbusiness empire is tying itself ever closer to the federal government just as he spends record sums to help decide who controls it in the2026 midterm election.

SpaceXhas racked up at least $6.78 billion in federal work so far through Oct. 1 this year, according to FedScout, a research firm that tracks government spending and contracts, nearly twice its total for all of 2024.Tesla, SpaceX, including Musk's artificial intelligence business, also face high-stakes government decisions over defense spending, launch licenses, spectrum, autonomous vehicles, electricity and data centers.

At the same time, Musk has committed roughly $366 million to the 2026 election cycle across at least 40 races, making the world's richest person the midterms'biggest individual donorso far.

At least $276 million of that money has flowed to Republican groups and Musk's own political operation, America PAC, since July, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings, as Republican candidates have been whacked on thecost of livingand the war inIran.

For Musk, Republican victories could help preserve his influence and a favorable political environment for his companies. Democratic control of either chamber could instead bring subpoenas and investigations into his businesses, federal contracts and his work leading PresidentDonald Trump'sDepartment of Government Efficiency.

Democrats are favored to win control of the House, while the battle for the Senate remains a toss-up.

"With all that spending, [Musk] wants favors in Congress and from the administration and influence on regulatory contracts as well as being shielded from oversight," saidBruce Freed, president and co-founder of the Center for Political Accountability and a former chief investigator for the Senate banking committee.

Musk did not respond to CNBC's request for a comment on this story. However, he lashed out at the possibility ofDemocrat-led investigationsin a Wednesday post on X, which he owns, saying: "Live by the sword, die by the sword."

"Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets," he wrote.

Nowhere is the overlap between Musk's business interests and political spending clearer than in his homestate of Texas.

Tesla is headquartered in Austin, where it operates its largest U.S. vehicle factory. SpaceX operates a launch facility at its company town, Starbase, in South Texas. Musk's tunneling venture, The Boring Co., is based in Pflugerville.

That gives Texas officials sway over taxes, electricity, permitting, infrastructure and economic-development incentives that can carry enormous consequences for Musk's companies.

At least $189.6 million of his political money is targeted to help elect RepublicanKen Paxtonthrough various avenues, prompting his Democratic opponent,James Talarico, to accuse Musk of trying to "buy this Senate seat in Texas."

Musk went after Talarico on Wednesday, saying on X that "There is something deeply wrong" with the Democrat.

"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator,"Talarico responded.

Musk is spending at the state level, too. He and his trust have given at least$6 millionthis cycle to state candidates and political groups, including Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and House Speaker Dustin Burrows.

The Musk-Abbott connection also extends to personnel: Tesla policy chief Karen Steakley previously served as Abbott's deputy director for legislative affairs.

Tesla and SpaceX are also planning to build a sprawling AI chip factory withInteloutside of Austin in Grimes County, Texas, where longtime Musk lawyer and America PAC attorney Chris Gober is running for Congress.

For SpaceX, the federal government is one of its most importantcustomers.

Since 2008, the company has received more than $30.7 billion in federal work, according to FedScout. The figure excludes classified contracts and some state-funded spending on services such as Starlink terminals and satellite internet service, which states have used during disaster recovery.

That federal business has accelerated during Trump's second administration, FedScout found. SpaceX has racked up $6.78 billion in 2026 so far, compared with $3.97 billion in 2025 and $3.8 billion for all of 2024.

In late May alone, the Space Force awarded SpaceX $2.29 billion for a military communications network tied toGolden Domeand, three days later, another$4.16 billionfor threat-detection satellites.

Congress does not award those contracts, but it funds and oversees the agencies that do, including the Defense Department and NASA, both major SpaceX customers.

"Keeping allies in committee powers in Washington helps [Musk] wield power in the halls of Congress better," saidHilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan research group that tracks money in politics.

Musk's America PAC is backing Sen.Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, which helps write funding bills for NASA and the Pentagon – two of SpaceX's biggest government customers.

Collins' Democratic opponent,Troy Jackson, has accused Musk of trying to "buy a government that serves his interests."

Musk has already learned how quickly that kind of political influence can evaporate.

After spending nearly $300 million to help elect Trump and congressional Republicans in 2024, Musk gained extraordinary access to the administration. He ledDOGE'spush to slash the federal workforce and pressed for deregulation on several fronts.

Then the relationship blew up. A June 2025 feud over Trump's tax-and-spending bill escalated into threats from the president to cut government support and contracts for Musk's companies.

Now Musk is back in Trump's orbit. In recent weeks, he has attended Trump's state dinner with Chinese PresidentXi Jinping, sat beside the president at hisAIsummit and received theNational Medal of Science. On Sept. 30, the DOD appointed Musk to co-leadProject Meridian, advising the Pentagon on future warfare.

Musk’s political spending extends well beyond the states where his business empire is concentrated.

Across six other battleground states,America PAChad spent about $22.7 million on general election expenditures through Oct. 20, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings, including roughly $8.9 million in Ohio, $7.2 million in Michigan and $2 million in Maine.

In Michigan, America PAC is paying for digital ads, mailers, printing and postage, and text and phone outreach supporting RepublicanMike Rogersand attacking DemocratAbdul El-Sayed, according to FEC filings.

Rogers backs a one-year moratorium on new data centers; El-Sayed wants to pause advanced AI development and newdata centersuntil tougher federal safeguards are in place.

In Ohio, America PAC is funding ads, text and phone outreach among other measures helping RepublicanJon Hustedagainst DemocratSherrod Brown, according to FEC filings. Husted wants large data centers to shoulder more grid costs; Brown has attacked industry tax breaks and pledged to make data centers pay their full electricity costs.

Those debates matter more as Musk pushes deeper into AI.

SpaceX's AI division, formerly known as xAI, was awarded aPentagon contractlast July with a $200 million ceiling, while a General Services Administration agreement makes the company'sGrokchatbot available across federal agencies through March 2027.

Musk's companies also depend on a web of federal regulators whose decisions can directly affect their ability to expand.

The Federal Aviation Administration licenses SpaceX launches, while the Federal Communications Commission controls satellite licenses and spectrum used by Starlink. Congress funds and oversees both agencies, and the Senate confirms FCC commissioners.

Tesla has its own stakes in Washington, where Congress and federal agencies can reshape electric-vehicle tax breaks, battery subsidies, autonomous-vehicle rules and trade policy affectingChinesecompetitors.

Musk's companies are spending directly on those fights, too.

Since January 2025, SpaceX has spent about$5.3 millionlobbying on issues including NASA funding, defense spending, military launches, missile defense and procurement, while Tesla has spent about$3.6 millionlobbying Washington, according to disclosure reports.

"Elon's spending is virtually unprecedented in recent elections for its scale in such a short period for one individual donor," Freed told CNBC. "He seems to be spending with basically no budget, and he got the money to do so."

title: Trump asked Musk to lift Starlink slowdown, WSJ reports
content:
PresidentDonald TrumpaskedElon Muskto ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version ofSpaceX's Starlink system in Ukraine, The Wall Street JournalreportedThursday, citing U.S. officials.

The Starshield system, which Ukraine depends on in its war against Russia, was "working more normally Thursday, shortly after" Trump spoke to Musk by phone, U.S. and Ukrainian officials told the Journal.

The newspaper reported Tuesday that Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX and a critic of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had ordered the Starlink slowdown.

Two unnamed sources in that report said Trump and Musk had discussed the decision to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, while one source said Musk had spoken to Trump prior to imposing the speed cap.

Trump has repeatedly denied involvement in the decision and said he does not know if Musk was behind it.

"I don't know who did it, but I was not involved," Trump said Wednesday.

The Starlink controversy, which drew bipartisan concern and criticism from lawmakers, emerged as Trump has ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy for continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure. At the same time, Trump has pursued a deal to ease sanctions on Russia so it can supply some diesel on the global market.

Sen.John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."

Sen.Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the ranking member of the Senate homeland security committee's investigations subcommittee, on Thursday launched an inquiry into how SpaceX's satellite tech was "degraded for Ukraine without notice."

"This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally not only put Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril, but raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," Blumenthal said inletters to Muskand Defense SecretaryPete Hegseth.

The White House and an email associated with Musk did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Thursday's report that Trump had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

This is developing news. Please check back for updates.

title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Meta chief executive Mark ZuckerbergByDearbail Jordan,ÂBusiness reporterÂandÂKali Hays,ÂTechnology reporterPublished22 October 2026, 17:16 BSTUpdated 2 hours agoMeta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (Â£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in Californiawas less than 1%,externaleach year.Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.Through what's known as a stock splitannounced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.'Critically important'Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.Layoffs havecontinuedinto this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.Major tech companies are set to spend anestimated $1 trillion,externalthis year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, likedata centres.Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.Related topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergFacebookArtificial intelligenceTaxMore on this storyMeta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacyPublished22 hours ago

title: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over
content:
From AI companies financing data center projects to France's heavily indebted government, credit markets are flashing warnings as investors grow warier of borrowing risks.

Five-year credit default swap spreads have widened forCoreWeave,OracleandSoftBank Group, as well as France and Italy, according to CNBC's analysis of FactSet data.

AI-related bonds have been selling off as markets raise the cost of capital amid concerns of a financing crunch. Neocloud demand is "off the charts," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangtold CNBCon Thursday, but he warned of a "scarcity of capital." "The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," he said, adding, "that's going to get solved."

Countries like France face a similar crunch. Pressure is building in bond markets as investors demand more compensation to finance public debt.Recent mass protests and riotingin France have heightened the market's concerns.

"Markets may no longer want to underwrite massive capex, heavy leverage, and uncertain future cash flows, and that same shift is widening French sovereign spreads as investors demand more compensation to hold long‑duration, debt‑financed obligations from a strained state,"  FedWatch Advisors CIO and founder Ben Emons wrote on his"French Neoclouds" Substack post.

CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are at the heart of the AI infrastructure buildout, spanning data centers, cloud services and financing.

Their five-year CDS spreads offer a window into investors' anxiety about the cost of it all and eventual payoff. Higher spreads mean more expensive default protection and can signal greater concern about a borrower's creditworthiness.

CoreWeave has experienced some of the sharpest increases in default-protection costs. Its five-year CDS spread reached 1,065.84 basis points on Oct. 21, according to FactSet, reflecting heightened concerns about the debt-heavy company's ability to finance its expansion.

At the same timeOracle's spread roseto 308.25 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 141 on Jan. 2. S&P Credit Ratings downgraded Oracle's debt to the lowest level of investment grade in July, citing the expanding infrastructure business raised the overall credit risk.

Softbank is a major AI investor with a large stake in OpenAI and investments in data centers and power infrastructure, including an $87 billioncommitmentfor data centers in France. Its five-year CDS spread stood near a four-year high of 432 basis points on Oct. 20, up from 284 basis points on Jan. 5.

France isn't in a full-fledged debt crisis, but markets are signaling unease with the cost of protecting against a sovereign default rising above that of Italy's, which has also increased.

France's five-year credit default swap spread reached 89.8 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 29.74 basis points on Jan. 2, according to CNBC's analysis. Italy's spread increased to 67.1 basis points on Oct. 22 from 28.33 on Jan 2. France's budget uncertainty and debt burden have become a focus, raising concerns that the risk could spill over to other countries in Europe.

Germany's spread also rose but remained much lower at 12.15 basis points on Oct. 22, compared with 7.47 at the start of the period.

Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, pointed to France's mounting debt burden and persistent fiscal deficits as key drivers of rising default-protection costs.

"The key drivers are the large amount of French sovereign debt (120% of GDP) and the inability to reduce the deficit," Wizman told CNBC. In comparison to France, German government debt is 65% of the country's GDP.

Investors are also watching the spread between French and German bonds, considered the European benchmark of creditworthiness, which has also surged to 1.6 percentage points. France's 10-year bond yield alsotopped 5% for the first timesince 2002. The spread between the 10-year yield on French OATs and German Bunds is the extra payment investors demand to hold French bonds instead of German.

While the Franco-German spread is relatively wide, the Eurozone saw far larger gaps in borrowing costs during theEurozone debt crisisof the early 2010s.

France faces another test on Oct. 23 whenMoody's is scheduled to review its Aa3 sovereign rating, which carries a negative outlook. The review comes as political divisions complicate efforts to repair the country's public finances.

While stresses are popping up in some pockets of AI financing, debt markets are also pricing in higher costs.S&P Global warnedon Oct. 19 that major cloud providers may have more AI-linked debt exposure than publicly recognized.

CDS indexes offer a broader picture of credit-market pressure by tracking default-protection costs across baskets of companies.

North America's CDX High Yield index captures credit risk across speculative-grade companies. Its five-year midpoint spread reached 355.35 basis points on Oct. 20, up about 39 basis points from the end of 2025, according to data from LSEG.

The widening suggests investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk beyond AI-linked borrowers.

title: Elon Musk reportedly invests about $1 billion in Skydance
content:
Elon Muskhas made an investment inSkydanceof roughly $1 billion, according to areport from Semafor Thursday.

The financial injection comes as the company looks to cut costs. Paramountclosed its acquisitionof Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6,naming the combined entity Skydance. Co-CEOs David Ellison andYnon Kreizare tasked with merging two major film studios in Paramount and Warner Bros., two popular streaming platforms — Paramount+ and HBO Max — and a host of corporate functions to support a portfolio of TV networks and two news divisions.

Skydance has said it expects to see $6 billion in cost savings over three years, though it faces a debt burden of nearly $80 billion.

Musk's commitment is part of a wider effort by Skydance to raise equity investments, Semafor reported. Representatives for Musk and Skydance did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

Shares of Skydance fell about 1% following the report.

Ellison's father, Larry Ellison, has a history with Musk. The Oracle co-founder invested $1 billion in Musk's 2022 deal to purchase Twitter, now called X. Larry Ellison also invested inTeslain 2018 and served on the company's board of directors.

The elder Ellison also personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of equity financing in Paramount's offer to take over WBD.

title: Bill Ackman says 2027 will be an amazing year for stocks as wars, inflation ease
content:
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman said two geopolitical conflicts — the Ukraine-Russia and Iran wars — along with elevated inflation and interest rates are holding back an otherwise "booming market environment."

"Once the overhang of the war is done — and it sounds like we're also potentially heading in the right direction with Russia-Ukraine — energy prices could come way down, and obviously that would be very good for inflation and markets," Ackman told CNBC's "Money Movers" on Thursday. "We're going to have an amazing 2027."

Ackman, who called the Iran conflict an "extremely well-executed war," believes that once there's peace in the Middle East, it will be great for the region and "ultimately great for the United States."

Higher crude prices have pressured stocks all year, as traders fear elevated energy costs will drive up inflation and force the Federal Reserve to raise rates. U.S. oil is up 72% in 2026, while Brent crude has surged 83%.

Rising oil appears to have trickled down to consumer prices. Gasoline prices accounted for over half of the increase in the latestconsumer price indexreport. Inflation has been stubborn, moving away from the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September.

Higher prices put the Fed in a bind to keep interest rates elevated to tame inflation.

Ackman also discussed individual long-term stock opportunities on his radar.

The hedge fund manager said he viewed Netflix'searningsfavorably. The streaming stock dropped more than 5% on Wednesday after reporting lackluster advertising and revenue guidance. On Thursday, however, they bounced more than 3%.

Ackman said that any concerns around Netflix's content library are overblown when considering the strength of its management team and its engagement with users. He added that the stock is currently trading at 18 times earnings, "one of the lowest valuations in history," and expected to post earnings growth in the mid to high teens for the foreseeable future.

"Netflix is a high growth utility," he said.

The billionaire investor also hasMeta Platformsas a core part of Pershing Square's portfolio.

Shares of the Facebook and Instagram parent are down 6% Thursday despite the companyreportingbetter-than-expected revenue in its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday, while issuing strong guidance for the current period.

The stock's drop didn't faze Ackman. "We're in a world in which you cannot look at the day one trading of a stock after earnings because of how levered market participants are and how short-term they are," he said.

"Meta is extremely well positioned in democratizing the use of agents," citing the company's success with its personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse.

Meta has "proven that AI is helping them accelerate their business and this remains an incredibly undervalued stock and that's why we own it," Ackman noted.

He unveiled his positionon the tech giant in February. At the time, Ackman cited Meta's "long-term upside potential from AI represents a deeply discounted valuation for one of the world's greatest businesses," during an investor presentation.

Ackman believes Meta's investments in compute infrastructure are necessary and could eventually generate attractive returns.

Ackman also reiterated his bullish stance on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, of which he is large shareholder in.

"These stocks will go up tenfold. and that's you know, that's the most asymmetric investment I'm aware of in the stock market," he said. "These entities have fully rebuilt their capital. What's not, I think, well understood is Fannie and Freddie today have five times the capital they had historically."

title: Musk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. Few exist
content:
Elon Musk's latest clash withUkraineunderscores the critical role thathis company's Starlinksatellite internet service has played in Kyiv's defense against Russia, which invaded unprovoked in 2022.

It's also laid bare the downsides of depending on a single provider for satellite internet communications, though other options are not yet comparable to SpaceX's Starlink and its military-grade Starshield offering.

On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officialsaccusedSpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself.

SpaceX and the U.S., they said, had suddenly and without warning imposed speed limits onStarshield. SpaceX describes Starshield as a "secured satellite network for government entities" that "leverages Starlink technology."

The changes cut wireless internet connectivity in drones and other aircraft moving at speeds over 100 mphthat Ukrainian forces were using in the campaign against Russia. A Ukrainian senior commander toldThe New York Timesthe Starlink restrictions cost his unit more than $1 million and delayed missions by three days.

Musk and PresidentDonald Trump, both critics of Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyy, have each shirked accountability for the communications disruptions in the war-torn nation.

On Tuesday,The Wall Street Journalreported that Musk individually ordered the service changes, and had discussed them with Trump before putting them in place.Trumpinsisted on Wednesday that he "was not involved."

Robert Weissman, who is co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, said the situation is an "extreme danger"that raises antitrust and security concerns around Musk's ability to control a "crucial means of communication."

"People worry about the political, as well as economic, impacts of oligarchy, and this is it," Weissman said in an interview. "It's not just that Musk can drown out other speakers, he can close down communications in a national security context for a country. No person should have that ability or power."

Thedisruptionshave prompted a bipartisan group of lawmakers in the U.S. to call for an investigation into Musk's actions, including calls for him to potentially testify under oath.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC on Wednesday that he doesn't believe Musk would have acted "without at least the acquiescence of the White House," and called attempts to throttle Starlink service in Ukraine "frankly shameful."

"There's a reason why we've had relative peace in Europe since World War II," Cornyn said in a "Squawk on the Street" interview. "And that's because of the alliance between the United States and our European allies. And I think anything we do to undermine that or degrade that is a big mistake."

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., called for an investigation on the matter and wrote, in asocial media postWednesday, "No billionaire, especially one that gets massive contracts from our government, should have the power to unilaterally decide to shut down communications and weapons during a war of critical importance to the US and Ukraine."

On SpaceX'searningscall this week, executives didn't address the issue and weren't asked about it by analysts.

Governments or companies looking for an alternative to Musk, SpaceX and its satellite internet services have few options.

Amazon'sLeo, which also delivers internet connectivity via a low Earth orbit satellite constellation, is seven years in the making and has yet to fully come online, with only390 satellitesin orbit.

SpaceX, by comparison, boasts a Starlink constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomerJonathan C. McDowell. Starlink connectivity is live in 174 countries, SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on Tuesday's earnings call.

Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos' space company, in January unveiled a service calledTeraWavefor enterprise and government customers. It's targeting deployment of the first batch of satellites in the fourth quarter of 2027.

France's Eutelsat, also a competitor to Starlink, has more than 600 satellites in orbit. Thestock surged23% on Oct. 14 as reports emerged that Musk had restricted Starlink in Ukraine.

Several countriesare looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is buildingIRIS², which is expected to span hundreds of satellites, but the first launches aren't expected until 2029.

Most of these planned systems are unlikely to "come anywhere close" in terms of capacity, coverage, resilience or cost compared to Starlink, said Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant. The cost, size, weight and power draw of Eutelsat's terminals make them particularly unsuitable in the battlefield, he added.

While SpaceX's Connectivity business has raced ahead of rivals, the company also has the advantage of overseeing a hugely successful rocket launch business, which has carried satellites to orbit for many of its competitors.

SpaceX is now phasing out commercial rides on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, while it tests and develops its massive Starship rocket.

Many new constellations "could therefore face substantial delays and materially higher launch costs," von der Ropp said.

This week, Ukraine and European lawmakers moved toexplore alternativesto Starlink, framing the issue as a matter of national security.

Their concern is that access to a critical communications service could potentially be disrupted "as a consequence of Musk's political agenda," said von der Ropp.

"The degree of soft power SpaceX has accumulated over companies, governments and militaries is substantial, and that has now become very visible," von der Ropp said. "Inevitably, this is creating mistrust and accelerating demand for alternatives."

Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday ina post on Xthat he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."

Musk enjoyed accolades for providingStarlinkterminals and satellite internet service during the early days of the war, but relations have soured between the world's richest person and Ukrainian officials over the years.

Musk previously ordered SpaceX engineers to shut off Starlink's satellite network over Crimea to thwart a Ukrainian attack on Russian warships, according to a chapter in the 2023 Musk biography written by Walter Isaacson. Musk disputed the report. The revelationdrew rebukefrom Ukrainian officials, including a top Zelenskyy aide, who said it led to Ukrainian civilians being killed.

"This is the price of a cocktail of ignorance and big ego," Mykhailo Podolyak, a top Zelenskyy advisor, wrote in a post on X, then known as Twitter.

Musk has also repeatedly argued that Ukraine should strike a "truce" with Russia andcede ownershipof Crimea, a strategically important territory, to Putin.

Musk's treatment of Ukraine played a part inCanada's decision to cut ties with Starlink. Officials inIndiaandTaiwanhave also expressed wariness of Starlink, citing national security concerns and preferring to adopt a mass communications service that's not controlled by SpaceX.

Musk lashed out at Indian "oligarchs" for stalling the Starlink rollout in the country.

He's also targeted some of Starlink's prospective enterprise customers.

Starlink has become the dominant provider for airlines' in-flight satellite Wi-Fi service, signing on dozens of carriers, includingUnited Airlines,Alaska Airlines,American AirlinesandSouthwest Airlines.

ButDelta Air Linesis one of the few carriers to choose Amazon's Leo service.

Earlier this month, Musk posted on X that Delta CEO Ed Bastian would "lose his job" over not choosing Starlink, following unconfirmed comments posted on X that Bastian told employees, "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me."

Bastian denied making the comment, and told CNBC on Oct. 9 that he's a "big fan" of Starlink and even drives a Tesla.

"All this nonsense about it being personal is not true at all," he said.

-- CNBC's Elsa Ohlen and Leslie Josephs contributed reporting to this story.

title: Lawsuit accuses Trump of illegally profiting off foreign crypto deals
content:
A lawsuit filed Thursdayaccuses PresidentDonald Trumpand his family'scryptocompany of "corruptly profiting" off more than $2 billion indigital currency-related deals, violating constitutional restrictions on accepting foreign money.

"No president in American history has profited from his office so brazenly," alleges the federal civil complaint from a shareholder ofCircle Internet Group, a publicly traded U.S. crypto company and competitor of the Trump family business,World Liberty Financial.

The suit filed in U.S. District Court in Washington by shareholder and former Circle employee J. Benjamin Greenberg centers on two allegedly "illegal foreign emoluments" involving World Liberty and Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security advisor to the United Arab Emirates.

Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon —widely known as the "Spy Sheikh"because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million.

The company toldThe Wall Street Journal, which revealed the transaction in January 2026, that Trump had no involvement in the deal. But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures.

The lawsuit also highlights a "scheme" by an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund chaired by Tahnoon to "inflate the value of President Trump's crypto holdings" through last year's purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty's stablecoin, USD1.

The lawsuit asserts the conduct violates the U.S. Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause, which forbids federal officeholders from accepting money or other gifts from foreign officials without the consent of Congress.

"What President Trump did is brazenly corrupt. He's made millions from these deals by selling out the American people," Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal, said in a statement to CNBC.

"We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," Pelikan said.

The suit says Greenberg is filing derivatively on behalf of Circle. The company said in a statement to CNBC it was not behind the lawsuit and does not comment on pending litigation."Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing," the company said via a spokesperson.

The suit names Trump, World Liberty and U.S. Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as defendants, as well as four related limited liability companies.

"World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations," David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesperson, told CNBC. "No one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government. These claims are without merit and we look forward to resolving them in court."

The White House and a spokesperson for Witkoff did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the lawsuit.

In addition to seeking a court declaration that Trump's profits violate the Constitution, Greenberg wants the president to disclose all other foreign crypto emoluments he's received and return any profits found to be illegal.

Trump and his family haverapidly expanded their crypto businesssince he returned to the White House. World Liberty Financial,launchedwith members of the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024, operates the USD1 stablecoin, and an entity affiliated with Trump and his family owns about 38% of the company.The business has been highly lucrative for Trump even as WLFI investors sufferedsteep losses. Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his2025 annual financial disclosure, including nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty. WLFI, meanwhile, fell from about 45 cents in August 2025 to about 5 cents by the end of June 2026.The venture has drawn particular scrutiny over its ties to the UAE. Months after Tahnoon's 2025 investment, the administration expandedUAE access to advanced U.S. AI chips, including for G42, a UAE state-backed AI company controlled by Tahnoon.U.S. lawmakers have sought information about those dealings and signaled that Trump family business transactions could face furtherinvestigationif Democrats gain subpoena power in Congress in the 2026 midterm election.

title: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
content:
Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.

Initial filingsfor unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.

That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.

Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.

Nonfarm payrollsrose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.

Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.

"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.

The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6.

Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue theirlatest decision on interest rates. Policymakers in recent days havecharacterized the labor marketas a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesomeinflation problemthat has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.

Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

Correction: The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6. An earlier version misstated the month and date.

title: Meta stock sinks 6% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative
content:
Metashares slumped roughly 6% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in itsthird-quarter earningsand raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures.

The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into itsartificial intelligencespending plans.

Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion to $145 billion.

Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter.

The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth."

Meta also said CEOMark Zuckerbergcould leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing.

Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted.

Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable to the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for.

—CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report.
