title: How Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia crippled the world’s second largest diesel supplier
content:
Ukraine launched massive drone assaults against Russia this week, hitting key oil infrastructure and signaling Kyiv intends to block the Kremlin from increasing diesel exports in defiance of President Donald Trump.

More than 1,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia on Sunday alone in one of the largest attacks this year, according tostate mediareports. The strikes set ablaze an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city and President Vladimir Putin's hometown.

Kyiv has ended its brief adherence to anenergy ceasefirethat Trump declared between Ukraine and Russia on Oct. 11. Moscow ignored that truce from the start and Kyiv vowed to retaliate.

Ukraine's drone strikes have achieved a scale, range and effectiveness that they have crippled Russia's diesel exports, said Tatiana Mitrova, an expert on the Russian oil industry at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy. Before the attacks, Russia was the second-largest diesel supplier in the world after the U.S.

As a result, Trump'sdealwith Putin to boost Russian diesel exports is likely dead in the water, said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler. "It seems unlikely that they'll be able to bring the volume of diesel back to the market that they are talking about without an energy ceasefire," Smith said.

Kyiv's strikes on Russian refineries and related oil infrastructure almost tripled to 31 in July compared to 11 in January, according to data from open-source intelligence firm Rochan Consulting in Warsaw, Poland.

The attacks slashed Russia's diesel exports by more than 75%, to 141,000 barrels per day (bpd) in September, compared to 608,000 bpd in the same period last year, according to Kpler data.

In response, Moscow banned exports in July to preserve domestic supplies. The Kremlin resumed shipments this month to fulfill the Trump-Putin deal.

Under Trump's diesel deal to relieve pressure on surging fuel prices, the Kremlin agreed to supply the global market with about 75,000 bpd in October and 124,000 bpd in November. But those export volumes are a rounding error compared to total demand, Mitrova said.

The Ukrainians are regularly launching swarms of drones now that number in the hundreds, compared to dozens earlier in the war, Mitrova said. They are also striking deeper into Russian territory, she said. In July, Kyiv hit Russia'slargest refinery at Omsk, deep in Siberia near the Kazakhstan border, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine.

And they have learned to target more complex refinery equipment that is harder to repair, Mitrova said. A destroyed fuel tank takes just a couple weeks to fix, she said. But replacing a secondary refining unit, for example, requires supply chains outside Russia, the analyst said.

"You cannot just order it on Alibaba," Mitrova said. "You need to make your order in advance and therefore securing this equipment quickly is not possible. You need to compensate for the risks of all the parties involved because [counterparties] are violating sanctions."

"You have to wait at least for several months if the right equipment is destroyed," she said.

With midterm elections less than two weeks away, Trump has blamed Ukraine for surging diesel prices that are jeopardizing Republicans' election chances.

Nationally, diesel cost $6.32 per gallon on average Tuesday, nearly 75% above the same period last year, according to AAA.

But the diesel market was already under pressure due to Trump's decision to go to war with Iran in late February. Tehran's attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and strikes by its Houthi militant allies on oil infrastructure of U.S. Gulf Arab allies has disrupted fuel exports from the Middle East.

Diesel exports through Hormuz, for example, are down about 540,000 bpd compared to last year, Kpler's Smith said. Global diesel exports have fallen about 1 million bpd due to lost supplies from Russia and the Middle East, he said.

Trump's options to reduce fuel prices are limited. The underlying problem is the shortfall of refining capacity due to damage from two wars that don't appear close to ending soon. U.S. refiners are already working at maximum capacity to fill the gap as much as possible.

The International Energy Agency warned this month that diesel supplies will likely remain constrained well into 2027. "The diesel tightness is likely going to persist in the coming months and prices are going to remain elevated," Smith said.

title: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are dominating the AI stock boom. Here's their edge
content:
Fueled by the global boom in artificial intelligence stocks, relaxed capital rules and greater lending to hedge funds, big Wall Street banks have already had a banner year for equities trading — even with one quarter left to go.

The five biggest investment banks have generated about $67 billion in equities revenue through Sept. 30, according to company filings. That is $7 billion more than what the group made during all of 2025, which itself was a record haul.

But it's Wall Street's Big Three that have captured the largest slice of what is shaping up to be the industry's most lucrative arena:Goldman Sachs,JPMorgan ChaseandMorgan Stanleyhave made a combined $52 billion in stock trading revenue so far this year, nearly 80% of the total.

"When it comes to the AI mega trade, the Big Three consider each other their main competitors, and that's pretty much it,"Mike Mayo, Wells Fargo banking analyst, told CNBC. "They've been best positioned to take advantage of this market."

Wall Street banks are experiencing an epic run of blockbuster profits as the total value of the stock market balloons and trading activity from institutional and retail investors rises across stocks, exchange-traded funds and derivatives. Helping drive this activity are the loans that the banks, through their prime brokerages, are extending to hedge funds so that they can amplify their bets.

Prime brokerage — the business of providing hedge funds with margin loans, securities lending and other trading services — has become a key battleground and source of growth. The Big Three's prime brokers are central to the larger equities story because they serve the largest funds across markets and products.

Demand for leverage to make bets on AI hardware, hyperscalers and chip suppliers has reached new heights, bank executives said last week.

At Goldman Sachs, equities financing activitiesjumped96% in the third quarter to a record $3.37 billion. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley don't break out that figure, but said they saw a similar dynamic.

"I like your 'insatiable demand for capital' point. That feels about right," JPMorgan CFOJeremy Barnumsaid on the bank's third-quarter conference call, responding to analyst questions about financing demands.

"In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme ... there is capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms," Barnum said.

That demand has helped transform equity desks at the Big Three from cyclical, transactional businesses into more durable, high-margin lending engines, Wall Street executives say.

The performance gap between Wall Street's giants and rivals includingBank of AmericaandCitigrouphighlights a widening divide in capital markets.

"For clients, the value isn't just a price on one trade, it's coverage and continuity,"Rachid Alaoui,JPMorgan global head of equities, told CNBC in an interview. "You want a dealer that can give you the full suite across products, and you want that service to travel with you across regions. That matters in stressed markets and periods of volatility."

Executing multibillion-dollar bets, like leveraged swaps on volatile AI stocks or sector ETFs, can require an enormous balance sheet. The biggest banks can absorb potential $100 million losses without threatening their quarters, according to trading executives. Smaller or more niche banks can't underwrite single-trade risks of that magnitude, forcing them to decline the business or cede share.

U.S. prime brokers have also benefited from theretreatof European banks includingCredit Suissefrom the equities business, said Bloomberg Intelligence analystHerman Chan.

"Prime is one of the ultimate scale businesses," Chan said. "If you have a strong equities franchise, the hedge funds will want to transact with you because you have a bigger pool of trading opportunities with counterparties."

While U.S. markets were swept up in software and cloud computing giants this year, trading executives say the fastest-growing frontier for equities was in Asia.

Institutional investors poured into South Korea and Taiwan, targeting the "picks and shovels" of the AI supply chain: the memory chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers supporting data center construction, Alaoui said.

For the Big Three, with their footprints across Tokyo; Hong Kong; Seoul, South Korea; and Mumbai, India; the Asia trade was a goldmine. However, trading executives point out that transaction taxes and stamp duties are included in top-line revenue, artificially inflating Asia prime totals.

There is also no agreed-upon definition of what equities trading revenue should include, so some banks include business lines like clearing services that others exclude from their stock trading totals, making apples-to-apples comparisons difficult.

But that doesn't change the overall momentum of the business, boosted by a stock rally that began in October 2022, weeks beforeOpenAIreleased ChatGPT.

"We're still in a stock-based world," Morgan Stanley CEOTed Picksaid on the firm's earnings call. "Equities are still, all things being equal, the attractive asset class."

While the CEOs of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have said the AI build-out is still in its early years, if AI turns out to be not as transformative as hoped, a downturn could impact those banks more than others, analysts said.

The boom has also drawn some concern over the possible risks posed by hedge funds.

The International Monetary Fundwarnedthis month thatgrowing leverage, crowded positions and correlated selling from hedge funds could create potential stability risks. The IMF estimated that global hedge fund assets had reached $13 trillion.

In August, JPMorgan CEOJamie Dimonsaid industrywide leverage was "thehighest it's ever been," though he stopped short of calling the risk big enough to pose a threat to the financial markets.

Wall Street executives and analysts pointed out that the industry wasn't fazed by the meltdown of several hedge funds this summer. While the hedge fund run by formerOpenAIresearcherLeopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness, garnered the most headlines, several smaller firms also experienced a forced unwinding.

Prime brokers have learned to leap on margin calls and quickly take down risk when markets move against clients, JPMorgan's Alaoui said.

"In the summer, some investors had positions they were forced to unwind," he told CNBC. "They deleveraged, risk came down, and the market moved on."

Another factor driving the equities boom: Trump administration regulators haveeasedsome leverage rules for the largest U.S. banks, giving them more room to expand balance sheet-heavy businesses including prime brokerage. The revised rules were finalized in 2025, and banks were allowed to adopt them as early as January.

By easing the stringent balance sheet caps that previously treated Treasurys and prime brokerage loans, which are collateralized, the same as riskier assets, regulators gave dealersgreater flexibilityto deploy balance sheet capital.

"Capital did go down, so you have to say the system is somewhat more levered because of the relaxation in regulations," saidDarrell Duffie, a finance professor at Stanford University and a leading expert on financial stability. "It's not a good idea, but it hasn't gotten dramatically out of whack."

The larger size of the market and higher volatility can create more trading, derivatives activity and leverage, he said, but that's not inherently alarming.

Wall Street executives also downplayed concerns over leverage, pointing out that they use collateral and frequent stress testing to get ahead of problems.

"Hedge fund leverage as a contributor of risk to the system is very much in the category of known unknowns," JPMorgan's Barnum said last week. "It doesn't mean it's riskless, but we kind of know what it is."

— CNBC'sLeslie PickerandRitika Shahcontributed to this report.

title: The political ad wars are still being fought over the airwaves even as digital gains share
content:
While advertising dollars increasingly shift towardstreaming and digital platforms, the political ad war is still being fought over the free airwaves.

Broadcast television companies are set to capture the greatest portion of political ad spend ahead of themidterm elections, according to advertising intelligence company AdImpact.

The 2025-26 election cycle is forecast to be themost expensive on record, with a predicted $11.6 billion in total spending. That's higher than the $11.2 billion spent on advertising during the 2024 presidential election cycle and the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms.

An estimated $5.6 billion of advertising spend ahead of the midterms, or 48%, is expected to go to broadcast companies, AdImpact found.

"It's still a local game," said StoneX Equity Research Analyst Daniel Kurnos in an interview. "Yes, there are national elections, but you have to win counties. And if you have to win counties, you have to reach voters in these counties."

Broadcast audiences — those tuning into NBC, ABC, CBS, Fox or their local affiliate stations — are generally more politically active, Kurnos said: "You cater to the demos that vote. You cater to the votes that matter."

That makes political advertising one of thelast bastionsof broadcast's dominance.

While broadcasters are expected to capture roughly half of political advertising spending this cycle, they account for just 7.7% of the more than $470 billion in general advertising spend forecast for this year in the United States, according to Magna data published by S&P Global in July.

Terry Nelson, a founding partner of Plus Communications and the national political director for former President George W. Bush's 2004 reelection campaign, told CNBC that broadcast spots allow political strategists to reach large numbers of voters "as efficiently as we can from a cost perspective."

Though cord-cutting has reshaped the TV landscape as customers drop cable, broadcast remains free and broadly accessible.

Broadcast, which transmits local news, sports, classic game shows like "Wheel of Fortune" and national networks, captured more hours of television use than cable in July, according to Nielsen's most recent monthly streaming report,The Gauge. The category accounted for 19.5% of television use, while cable captured 18.7%. Streaming led television use by far, at 49%.

Broadcast is still particularly good at delivering high viewershipduring live sports games,Nelson noted.

"If you think about an NFL audience, for example, you're still going to deliver big audiences amongst large segments of the population," he said. "So no matter how you dice that demographic, whether it's men, women, or old people, young people, or whatever the case might be, the NFL game is still going to deliver large segments of all of those audiences."

Brad Seitter, CEO of TVB, a trade organization representing the local broadcast industry, boiled down broadcast's strength during election cycles to "trust, reach and because it works."

Seitter told CNBC in a statement that television's perceived reliability is of utmost importance for political campaigns.

"Gaining the trust of a voter equals a vote for your candidate or issue," Seitter said.

He also said that he believes broadcast does a better job of promoting political candidates and issues than some digital channels.

"You may see a political ad on social media, but you don't trust the content of the ad because users are conditioned to not trust what they hear or see on social media," Seitter said. "Conversely, viewers trust their local broadcast TV news, so when they view a political ad, they are more likely to believe the content of the ad on a platform they know has long-standing rules, regulations and trust."

Seitter said that political campaigns continue to place advertisements on traditional TV because there is clear evidence that they are influential on voting behavior.

"Nothing moves the needle in polling like running an ad on broadcast TV," Seitter said.

According to a study conducted by TVB, 42% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans said broadcast or cable television was the most important form of advertising media in influencing how they cast their vote.

Erik Brydges, head of performance and political demand at sell-side ad company Magnite, told CNBC that broadcast's perceived influence is tied to the long history of the platform.

"There are multiple studies out there that show a correlation between the number of points you buy on TV in relation to moving poll numbers, because the medium's been around for like 70 years," he said.

And yet Brydges said he believes that broadcasting's strength is also due, in part, to muscle memory.

"A lot of campaigns and a lot of the consultants who work on the campaigns have just been really used to buying TV," Brydges said. "There's an old adage out there that no political consultant is ever going to get fired for suggesting buying more TV."

Broadcast companies are already feeling the windfall from elevated advertising spending.

Publicly traded broadcasters, includingNexstar Media Group,Gray Media,SinclairandE.W. Scripps, each reported high political advertising revenue in their most recent fiscal quarters and forecast continued growth through the fall as the midterms inch closer.

StoneX's Kurnos told CNBC that broadcasting companies rely on the low-lift revenue from political advertising to help manage their debt.

"They have all the infrastructure in place for [standard advertising] already," Kurnos said. "And you don't need to work on the creative. You don't need to work on the selling. … Political is just, therefore, pure margin dollars."

Nexstar, which owns or operates at least 265 stations and a slew of websites and mobile apps,reported its highest quarterly revenuein the company's history. Net revenue hit $1.99 billion, and advertising revenue was $862 million, according to the August earnings report.

Overall revenue in the second fiscal quarter was largely driven by the incorporation of broadcast rival Tegna, whichNexstar officially acquired in March.

However, even discounting additional revenue from the merger, the company still reported fiscal second-quarter growth at legacy Nexstar that was primarily driven by $75 million of political advertising revenue, according to the company's most recent earnings call.

Gray Media, though operationally smaller than Nexstar, could also be a company to watch, according to Kurnos.

The company's stations operate in several markets with the most competitive races and thus the greatest ad spend: Gray has exposure in 12 competitive Senate races and all 11 competitive gubernatorial races, according to Kurnos.

"Gray has always been the most efficient political generator of the broadcast group," he said.

SinclairandScrippsalso reported political ad revenue as a bright spot in their earnings reports for the most recent fiscal quarter.

E.W. Scripps said that political ad revenue hit the highest second-quarter level ever, while Sinclair said that political ad revenue had grown 9% from the second quarter of 2022 during the last midterms season.

"No other medium delivers a political message as powerfully and reliably as broadcast television," E.W. Scripps CEO Adam Symson said on the company's second-quarter earnings call.

On the other end of the media spectrum, connected TV represents the fastest-growing category of political advertising spend, according to AdImpact. The category encompasses internet-connected devices likeAppleTV orRoku.

It's predicted to capture 23%, or $2.7 billion, of this cycle's ad spending, AdImpact found, and is likely to continue to gain share.

Magnite's Brydges said the complicated and rapidly changing nature of connected TV, or CTV, and free, ad-supported streaming channels — also called FAST — has prevented some advertisers thus far from taking advantage of high viewership numbers.

"If you look at some of the FAST streaming services — some of your Plutos, your Tubis — a campaign or a consultant might not understand what those are," Brydges said. "Therefore, they might just be like, 'Well, if I don't understand what it is, then it's probably not worth investment.'"

However, he said he believes political consultants are becoming more attuned to the benefits that these platforms provide.

SKDK's Pia Carusone, who manages the firm's political advertising department, told CNBC in an interview that she sees value in streaming's specific audience targeting features.

"If you're buying NBC in New York City, for example, you're buying the whole market," she said of traditional advertising strategy. "Increasingly, now with the streaming and CTV platforms, they're able to really offer a lot more nuance in their targeting. So we're able to sort of deliver against those audiences more directly."

But ultimately, Carusone said, political advertising strategy relies on maintaining a diverse portfolio.

"You can't just do digital. You can't just do linear," she said. "Good buyers today are buying across the spectrum."

title: United Airlines set to open its biggest airport lounge in $2.6 billion overhaul at Houston hub
content:
United Airlinesis set to open its biggest airport lounge this week, which it says is the largest in the Americas, as airlines continue to plow money into the facilities for high-spending customers.

The 54,000-square-foot lounge is opening Thursday at George Bush Intercontinental Airport's Terminal B in Houston, part of an overhaul of the facility that includes 22 gates for mainline aircraft.

The airport, with more than 500 departures a day, is United's main connecting hub for flights to and from Latin America.

The new club can seat 800 people and features an outdoor terrace for plane-spotting as well as two full-service bars and buffets.

The lounge, part of United's $2.6 billion investment at the airport's Terminal B, shows how airlines are putting more money intolarger spacesfor premium-travel demand to attract the growing ranks of elite frequent flyers, co-branded credit card holders and customers just willing to spend more to fly.

American Airlinesearlier this month said it is planning its largest-ever lounge at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport hub in North Carolina.Delta Air Lineshas expanded both its popular Delta Sky Clubs and its top-tier Delta One Lounges.

Southwest Airlinesis building its first-ever network ofairport lounges, which are tied to its credit card partner,Chase. Last week, the carrier unveiled mock-ups of the lounges, which it is calling Icon. AndJetBlue Airwaysopenedloungesin New York and Boston in the past year.

title: Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck
content:
Nvidiaannounced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing.

The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said.

"The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week.

The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers.

Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analystssaya single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million.

The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027.

Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated.

"What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang saidrecentlyon a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up."

title: House committee says Webull messages point to China access to U.S. customer data
content:
Internal messages between employees of online investing platformWebullsuggest a company employee inChinahad access to information about a U.S. customer, despite the company having said it bars such sharing, according to an analysis of the messages by theHouse Select Committee on China.

The analysis comes nearly two weeks afterCNBCfirst detailed the bipartisan select committee'sreportthat concluded that Webull, which counts 28 million users, is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to American finance.

Webull shares slid more than 19% on the heels of thatOct. 7 report.

At the time of the report, Webull told CNBC in a statement that "U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S."

But the newly released internal messages by the House Select Committee on China, which CNBC exclusively obtained, raise questions about whether that has always been the case.

The committee has focused on threats posed by China and protecting U.S. industry from Chinese competition.

One message thread suggests a Webull employee was in China during a discussion about a U.S. customer account.

The thread also indicates the account was previously approved by a China Webull team member and an American counterpart.

The messages, dating to 2021, were sent on Microsoft Teams between Brendan Fuller, a manager at Webull's U.S. brokerage, and an employee named Zhenghan Wang, whose nickname is "Rock."

The select committee says Wang was likely in China at the time.

In one message, Fuller messaged Wang about concerns involving a particular trading account.

"We saw these problems ... and approve account," Fuller wrote.

CIP is an acronym for Customer Identification Program, a U.S. regulatory requirement that financial institutions verify the identities of individuals and entities opening accounts.

"I thought so," Fuller responded.

Wang asked Fuller: "Who approve the account?"

Fuller responded: "One China team member and one US team."

Wang then asked: "I want to know in what situation (CIP), can we approve the account open?"

Fuller responded: "I think we just approve them all no matter what ..."

"And then we pay for vendors. And create report and work," Fuller added.

Wang then replied that "CIP=" followed by Mandarin Chinese characters forming a common phrase that translates as "Exists in name only," or "Useless."

A spokesperson for the select committee, in a statement to CNBC, said, "All the evidence in these text messages points to Zhenghan Wang, a Webull employee, being located in China with access to U.S. customer data at the time he worked for the company."

An analysis by the committee concluded that Wang was in China at the time of the exchange because the messages' time stamps indicated that Wang was working daytime hours in Beijing, and because he set his software to translate the messages into simplified Chinese.

A Webull spokesperson did not directly respond to CNBC's questions about Wang's access to U.S. customer data in 2021 and whether that disproved the company's assertion that its U.S. data does not go to China.

The Webull spokesperson said, "Protecting customer data is central to Webull's operations."

"Webull's U.S. customer data is stored only in the U.S. on AWS servers in Virginia and Oregon, with access to sensitive data restricted to U.S.-based employees," the spokesperson said.

"U.S. broker-dealer operations are directed exclusively by U.S.-based personnel, and no individuals based outside the U.S. have ever exercised operational or decision-making authority over Webull's U.S. broker-dealer business."

The company spokesperson also criticized the select committee's release of the messages.

"The Teams messages now being referenced date back to a 2021 routine FINRA matter, which was concluded," the spokesperson said. FINRA, or the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, is the self-regulatory organization for member broker-dealers.

The messages' "recent disclosure, alongside the Select Committee's report relying on preliminary and outdated information, raises legitimate questions about the timing and circumstances surrounding their release," Webull's spokesperson said.

"Webull rejects irresponsible speculation and stands on our well-documented record: Webull's data protection practices are robust, continuously enhanced, and independently verified."

The select committee's Oct. 7 report argued that Webull's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. Those Chinese laws can compel firms to cooperate with the government in various ways, including mandating data transfers.

The select committee on Tuesday issued a press release titled, "The Facts on Webull's Ties to China."

The release said that since the committee issued its report, Webull "has ... responded with numerous false statements about its business and its interactions with the Select Committee."

The committee listed five claims by Webull, followed by what the committee labeled "The Truth."

One section, titled "Webull Claim: 'U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S.,'" was followed by a rebuttal that said, "The Truth: The Select Committee's report does not dispute where the data is stored.

"Its finding is about who can reach the data and the systems that process it," the committee continued. "The report found that Webull affiliate Webull Technologies Limited previously used Tencent Cloud, a China-based provider, to host certain user data ... Webull has not said what data Tencent hosted or when that ended."

Webull said Tuesday that it was partnering withKalshi, the prediction market platform, to offer so-calledperpetual futuresto U.S. customers.

The first set of perpetual futures, which do not have an expiration date, as traditional futures do, would be for cryptocurrencies, Webull said.

title: 'MAKE DEALS': Trump says data centers should pay communities a 'dividend' to win support
content:
U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpon Wednesday urged data center companies to "MAKE DEALS" with local communities to ensure their support for the costly facilities.

Trump said that to make them more popular, data center operators should pay the community, "and/or individuals within the community, a 'dividend.'"

"I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.," the president said in a post on Truth Social.

Data centers have become ahot-button issueahead of the midterm elections in November.Public oppositionto the buildout of the facilities and their environmental impact has been growing, with multiple states considering moratoriums.

AI infrastructure companyNebiusis "100% in principle" having discussions about investing in communities, the company's Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky told CNBC when asked about Trump's suggestion of a dividend.

There could be "some sort of way where the rewards are actually funneled back to the community," Boroditsky told CNBC'sArjun Kharpalon the sidelines ofNvidia's GTC Berlin conference.

"We see it today in terms of the tax revenue that are arriving. I could see something like a benefit of some sort that's more direct economic opportunity for the community as well," he said.

Boroditsky added: "A dividend is being paid in different forms — investing in education, job development, overall economic development. The concept that the president identified... it's not crazy to consider something like that."

Data center stocks have also come under pressure this week amid growing concerns about the financial health of the sector. As the AI infrastructure buildout grows more costly, companies are increasingly turning to debt markets to finance deals.

When it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology,HSBCCEO Georges Elhederyadvised discernmentover an all-in approach.

"One has to be selective," Elhedery told CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."

Much of the concern centers aroundwater usage,power consumption, electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. Access to power is a major constraint on the sector, as power grids in the U.S. and Europe become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.

"Energy is always a bottleneck, and trying to find powered land and areas that we can build large-scale AI factories is a big focus for us," Chase Lochmiller, CEO of compute infrastructure firm Crusoe, told CNBC Wednesday in Berlin.

"Increasingly there's a lot of policy permitting and just working through local communities to make sure that everything can come online effectively," he said.

Trump, along-time supporterof data centers, said Wednesday that he has been watching them "very closely" and has now come to a "very strong conclusion."

"New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data  enters are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease," Trump said, in a post around 1.37 a.m. ET.

In some cases, data centers can operate as flexible loads, adjusting their electricity use to help stabilize the grid.

Hyperscalers havesecured dealswhere they agree to help finance badly needed updates to local power grids. However, some experts have warned that the AI boom will ultimately result inhigher electricity prices.

title: Witkoff heads to Russia for Putin talks as Zelenskyy insists 'nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine'
content:
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff is holding talks with Russian PresidentVladimir Putinabout ending the war in Ukraine, a day after Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyinsisted that any negotiations over his country's future must include Kyiv.

Speaking alongside the leaders of Finland and Norway in Oslo late on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said discussions with U.S. officials had been constructive and that Washington had reaffirmed its commitment to providing Ukraine with security guarantees.

But he stressed that any agreement concerning Ukraine's future would be acceptable only if Kyiv had a seat at the negotiating table.

"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said, adding that he had discussed thereported proposal of a trilateral meetingbetween the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the almost five-year conflict with U.S. representatives. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.

At the start of talks in St. Petersburg, Russia announced it would release an American man who had been "wrongfully detained," according to the State Department, on charges that he was a Ukrainian mercenary. Witkoff thanked Putin for the release of retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, according toRussian media.

On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Oslo meeting had included discussions on NATO's Article 5 – which says that an armed attack against one member constitutes an attack on all – and "different kinds of security guarantees," which Witkoff will share with the Russians. "We will hear his feedback in one day," Zelenskyy said Tuesday.

The developments come amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine as PresidentDonald Trumpand Zelenskyy have traded public criticism. Trump has accused the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace, while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia, including adeal on diesel, risks prolonging the conflict.

Overnight, Russia struck energy and civilian targets across Ukraine, resulting in at least one casualty, according to local media reports. It follows Trump's Oct. 11 claim that he had brokered an"energy ceasefire,"whereby the countries would refrain from striking each other's energy infrastructure amid high diesel prices.

Ukraine paused such attacks for three days before resuming them, citing continuing Russian attacks.

On Tuesday, Zelenskyy confirmed that U.S. intelligence had resumed sharing early warnings of Russian attacks, while discussions continued overSpaceX'sStarlink connectivity and Patriot air defense systems.

title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByFaisal IslamEconomics editorPublished21 October 2026, 11:03 BSTUpdated 52 minutes agoThe Chancellor was on a early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.The National Debt has topped Â£3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.Cost of living trade offThe latest inflation figure also applies as the uprating to tens of billions in welfare payments next April.By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.The figure also confirms that the Triple Lock will see the State Pension increase by 3.9% next April.There is one form of relief here - food price inflation remains largely unaffected by the energy shock.While higher inflation at a time of frozen tax thresholds will raise more tax in cash terms, it will also increase the cost of public services, including likely union pay demands.All the while, UK borrowing costs have risen alongside most of the advanced world as the US-Israel war against Iran has intensified.The Jackdaw gas field decision is seen as the start of a run of "pro growth" pre-Budget announcements.It sends a directional message, but will not fundamentally change the trade off between cost of living breathing space, and delivering a Budget that convinces the markets and investors.The fact the borrowing costs gap has narrowed a bit with other G7 nations, and the IMF praised pencilled-in plans to shrink borrowing, provided a platform for the chancellor's Budget.The latest economic numbers amply illustrate the challenge of actually delivering them.Related topicsInflationUK economyJohn HealeyHM Treasury

title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
content:
OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so.

An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks.

"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.

Warnings about the risksof developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.

The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.

OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

title: Stock futures rise as traders evaluate latest raft of earnings; SpaceX shares surge: Live updates
content:
U.S. stock futures were up early Wednesday as traders weighed the latest round of earnings reports.

S&P 500 futuresgained 0.29% andNasdaq-100 futuresadded 0.7%. Dow futures were flat.

In Asia, South Korea's Kospi advanced 2.7%, rebounding from Tuesday's losses. Japan'sNikkei 225was up 0.8%. The Hang Seng index declined 0.35%, while mainland China was flat. Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was little changed.

Shares of Elon Musk'sSpaceXjumped 8% after the company said its revenue grew 161% in the third quarter. Musk also said that SpaceX andTesla, his auto manufacturer, have formed special committees to discuss a merger. Tesla shares were up 1%.

In regular trading, theDow Industrialsadvanced nearly 530 points, or 1%, buoyed by a post-earnings jump in3M. Shares gained more than 5% after the industrial products company raised itsfull-year guidancefor profit. TheS&P 500gained 0.3%, while theNasdaq Compositeended the session marginally lower.

Oil prices ended the session slightly lower.West Texas Intermediate crude futuresslipped 1.8% on the day, whileBrent crude futureslost 0.7%.

This earnings season could help propel stocks as the year winds down, according to Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of asset allocation for Goldman Sachs Research.

"Near term there might be more volatility due to [artificial intelligence] concerns, Middle East tensions and midterm elections, but we think earnings support with lighter positioning and lower valuations should help equities into year-end," hewrote in a note.

Concerns around the sustainability of the AI trade have weighed on market sentiment, with traders focusing ondebt-backedAI investmentsand whether the infrastructure demand justifies companies' spending. Data storage playSeagate Technologyadded 2% in Tuesday's regular trading, while neocloud stockCoreWeaveadvanced more than 1%.

On Wednesday, investors can expect some more insight into the AI trade, with Meta Platforms due to report after the bell. Earlier this month, the company rolled out itslatest AI model, Muse Wonder, which is only available to paying users.

Traders are also watching for results from Tesla, IBM and Southwest Airlines, all due Wednesday.

Shares inAdidasrose 3.3% in premarket trading after the German sportswear giant's preliminary third-quarter operating profit soared 37% to 1.01 billion euros ($1.13 billion).

Revenues increased 9% to 7.25 billion euros, as the firm revised its full-year operating profit up to 2.5 billion euros, from 2.3 billion.

The company said Thursday that its gross margin reached 54.3% in the three-month period, boosted by about 200 million euros in U.S. tariff refunds.

Stoxx 50futures were 0.42% higher as European stock markets were expected to start Wednesday's session in positive territory.

Germany'sDAXis seen opening 0.45% higher, with Italy'sFTSE MIBadding 0.32% and the FrenchCAC 40rising 0.22%.

In the U.K.,FTSE 100futures were up almost 0.21%.

Shares of Australia'sNextDCplunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operatorslashedits annual earnings forecast, citing power supply delays at its Melbourne facility amid local community and stakeholder opposition.

The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million.

Shares of Chinese battery giant CATL fell 9.1% in Hong Kong and 9.2% in China on Wednesday after the company released its third-quarter results on Tuesday.

The companyreporteda 14.5% year-on-year rise in third-quarter net profit attributable to shareholders to 21.25 billion yuan ($3.18 billion), while revenue jumped 58.6% to 165.22 billion yuan.

Citi maintained its Buy rating on CATL but cut its 2026–2028 earnings forecasts by 9%, 14% and 15%, respectively, and lowered its price target for the company's Shenzhen-listed shares to 479 yuan from 500 yuan.

The bank said CATL's third-quarter net profit missed its expectations, citing weaker gross margins, higher expenses and impairment losses.

South Korea's stock exchange briefly halted program trading after Kospi 200 futures surged 5%, triggering a so-called "sidecar" mechanism designed to curb excessive market volatility.

The five-minute trading curb came as South Korean equities staged a sharp rebound on Wednesday, with technology and semiconductor stocks recovering from a bruising sell-off earlier this week as investors assess prospects of the artificial-intelligence sector.

The benchmark Kospi Index was up 4.4%.

Japan's exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing market expectations by a huge margin. Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%.

This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown, after hitting a near four-year high in July.

Growth was supported by continued strong semiconductor exports, with shipments rising 49.4% year on year by value.

Exports of machinery also bolstered growth, with semiconductor-related machinery shipments up 43.9% and power generation machinery exports climbing 22.6%.

In terms of destinations, shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%.

Asian technology stocks staged a broad rebound on Wednesday as optimism surrounding SpaceX's latest quarterly results helped revive sentiment toward artificial intelligence infrastructure investments following a bruising selloff.

South Korean memory chip giant SK Hynix surging 6.38%, while rival Samsung Electronics climbed 5.03%.

Shares of South Korean artificial intelligence infrastructure provider Elice soared 29.92%, recovering ground after plunging over 30% in its trading debut Tuesday. The sharp reversal came after the company's disappointing debut reignited concerns over whether heavy spending on AI infrastructure would translate into sustainable profits.

Japanese semiconductor stocks also rallied, with chip-testing equipment makerAdvantestjumping 5.31%, whileTokyo Electrongained 3.02%. Technology investment giantSoftBank Grouprose 4.70%.

"The SpaceX quarter and what this indicates for the neoclouds is very bullish globally and the Korean stocks have sold off way too much in my view," said Dan Ives, Tech Analyst at Yorkville Ives.

Asia-Pacific markets opened higher on Wednesday, with South Korean stocks leading gains.

The Kospi advanced 1.8%, rebounding from Tuesday's losses, while the tech-focused Kosdaq Index jumped over 2%.

Japan'sNikkei 225was up 1.4%, while the Topix added 0.93%.

Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was flat.

Asia-Pacific markets were set to open higher Wednesday, after Wall Street rose overnight on the back of strong corporate earnings and easing oil prices.

Futures for Japan'sNikkei 225in Chicago were at 65,355, while in Osaka they were lats at 65,210, compared with the index's previous close of 64,075.42

Futures for Hong Kong'sHang Seng indexlast traded at 24,001, higher than the index's last close of 23,867.74.

Australia'sS&P/ASX 200gained 0.27%.

Intuitive Surgical— The medical robotics stock fell about 7% as the company's third-quarter results failed to impress investors. Intuitive Surgical earned $3 per share, excluding certain items, on revenue of $3.05 billion.

SpaceX— Shares gained almost 7% after the Elon Musk-led rocket company reporteda 161% jump in third-quarter revenueto $14.58 billion. Musk also said that SpaceX andTesla, his auto manufacturer, have formed special committees to discuss a merger. Tesla shares were up 1%.

Netflix— Shares of Netflix fell more than 5% after the streaming giant reported third quarter revenue that was in line with Wall Street's expectations. Sales came in at $12.87 billion, up 12% year over year, boosted by growth in membership and anincrease in subscription pricesthat went into effect in March, the company said.

Read more about Tuesday's after-hours movers here.

U.S. stock futures were up Tuesday night as traders weighed the latest round of earnings reports.

Futures tied to theDow Jones Industrial Averagerose 0.19%.S&P 500 futuresgained 0.47% and Nasdaq-100 futures added nearly 1%.

title: Samsung, SK Hynix upgrading China plants to make more advanced chips, people say: Reuters
content:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are upgrading their China factories to produce more advanced memory chips, four people familiar with the plans said, aiming to fend off competition from a fast-growing Chinese rival and meet huge AI demand.

How much to invest in their Chinese operations has become a tricky question for the South Korean semiconductor giants ever since the US began imposing export controls on some chip-making equipment in 2022 amid an effort to slow China's technological progress.

Both companies are now required to seek US licenses annually if they want to install US-made equipment such as etching machines in China. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security also said in 2025 it did not intend to grant licenses to upgrade technology and expand capacity at the foreign chipmakers' factories in China.

The regulatory headaches have limited their ability to refit their factories and contributed to loss of market share to Yangtze Memory Technologies Co (YMTC). Executives at the South Korean chipmakers have publicly warned that geopolitical tensions are undermining their Chinese operations.

Samsung and SK Hynix confirmed in statements to Reuters that upgrades were underway and were being done in close consultation with Washington, but did not disclose details of production plans that are being reported here for the first time.

Reuters could not, however, determine to what extent US authorities have granted export licenses for equipment that Samsung and SK Hynix need for their planned upgrades.

According to the people, the two companies are working to manufacture flash NAND memory chips with more than 200 layers at their Chinese plants, which would bring them in line with what is being produced in South Korea.

NAND, a type of memory chip that retains data without power, is widely used in smartphones, PCs and solid-state drives for AI data centers. More layers per chip means more storage density and lower costs.

Samsung's plant in Xian in northwestern China, which accounts for about 40% of the company's global NAND output, currently makes chips that have about 200 layers, according to two of the people.

As part of a project known internally as "Monami" — from the French for "my friend" — Samsung is converting the facility to make 286-layer V9 NAND chips, aiming for monthly output of 5,000 wafers in December this year and then a jump to 40,000 wafers by December 2027, one of the people said.

Samsung said its upgrade was in compliance with US export regulations, adding: "The upgrade is aimed at meeting growing demand from global customers, including those in the US. The company is not expanding production capacity or constructing new manufacturing facilities."

SK Hynix is looking to switch to producing NAND products with 240 layers or more at its Dalian facilities in northeastern China, three people familiar with the matter said.

It currently makes products with 192 layers there, one person said.

SK Hynix acquired the Dalian site when it bought Intel's NAND operations in 2021 and it remains the sole NAND chip manufacturing site for that business, which is now named Solidigm and is preparing for a US initial public offering.

One of the people said the company is authorized to make chips with up to 240 layers at Dalian and may seek permission from Washington to conduct research and development on 300-plus-layer chips there that would help it lay the groundwork for potential production in the US. The company is in discussions with the Trump administration over plans to build a new NAND factory in the United States.

The US government's Bureau of Industry and Security did not directly address Reuters questions on the status of approvals for the South Korean chipmakers. It referred Reuters to its 2025 statement that the bureau intended to grant license applications for them to operate their existing factories in China, but not expand capacity or upgrade technology.

As Samsung and SK Hynix have wrestled with the question of how much to invest in their Chinese plants, YMTC has made great strides.

It commanded 38.5% of China's NAND market in the second quarter, up from 28% for all of 2025 and overtaking Samsung, according to research firm Omdia. In contrast, Samsung's share has slipped to 33.5% from 36% while SK Hynix's share has dropped to 17% from 20%.

YMTC's product lineup is mostly 160- and 232-layer NAND chips, but it also produces a small amount of 294-layer chips and plans to manufacture products with more than 300 layers, according to two separate people.

YMTC did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Outside China, Samsung sells NAND chips with up to 286 layers and it also unveiled a prototype NAND chip with more than 400 layers in August. SK Hynix sells NAND chips that are up to 321 layers.

title: Oil prices climb as traders assess Middle East developments
content:
Oil prices climbed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment.

Brent crude futuresgained 1.22% $110.13 a barrel, whileU.S. West Texas Intermediatecrude rose 1.11% to $98.92 a barrel.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized.

"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their officialSepah News website.

Adding to regional worries, Yemen's Houthi militants claimed responsibility on Monday for strikestargeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu,the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha.

The escalating tensions have also sent global oil shipping costs soaring, adding another layer of pressure to energy markets.

The global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel, compared with just $3 a year earlier, according to a Goldman Sachs report published Tuesday. While rates have eased slightly in recent days, they remain roughly seven times higher than a year ago.

Goldman estimated that war-risk premiums associated with crossing the Strait of Hormuz accounted for about $7 of the $20 year-on-year increase in average crude freight rates, while ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf contributed another $4.

The investment bank warned that elevated shipping costs could widen price differences between crude grades, squeeze refiners' profit margins and ultimately push up refined fuel prices.

"High freight costs have weighed particularly heavily on Asian refineries' net margins, threatening their refined product output, which could then raise global refined product prices," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.

title: U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plant
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will discuss refining Western energy supplies with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani'sReliance Industrieswhen he visits the company's plant in Jamnagar, Gujarat — the world's largest single-site refinery.

The U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance for refining energy from the "Western Hemisphere," Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18, which is owned by Reliance. "I think that's helpful to India, but it's also helpful to us," he added.

Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which Rubio will visit on Wednesday, has a crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Reliance has also emerged as thebiggest buyer of Venezuelan crudeoutside of the U.S., as of end-September.

The company's "extraordinary" refining capacity could help India diversify its energy supplies, Rubio said, hinting at possibly greater offtake of Venezuelan crude.

"We think there's an opportunity for them [Reliance Industries] to continue to help India diversify its supply chain, its supply of energy," Rubio said, adding that Venezuela was ramping up energy production, and that "India has had a long history of being able to refine some of that."

U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing India to buymore Venezuelan oilto replace Russian barrels, and while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer.

Beyond oil purchases, Reliance has been deepening ties with the U.S. this year, with Trump announcing in March that America will build its first new oil refinery in 50 years, helped by investment from Ambani's Reliance.

While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS AHISTORIC$300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY."

Reliance has never made an announcement about the refinery investment, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC, adding that it creates an air of uncertainty around the deal. Rubio would seek to "clinch" that deal or take it a little further, Chaudhuri said.

Rubio told Network 18 that Reliance had "invested in increasing the refining capacity within the United States."

His visit to Jamnagar also comes at a time whendiesel priceshave surged in the U.S., with midterm elections looming. Diesel prices, which affect American truckers, farmers, and shippers, are expected to remainelevated going into next year.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rubio underscored Reliance'sability to refine heavy crudeand referred to India as a "refining superpower" when asked about the role New Delhi and its companies can play in meeting the world's energy demand.

Indian and Chinese refineries are good at handling heavy and medium-heavy crude from Venezuela and Russia, Chaudhuri said, adding that this grade of fuel is better-suited for producing diesel.

title: Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX?
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished1 hour agoElon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he isconsidering bringing them together.Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (Â£1.1bn) and SpaceX at $2tn (Â£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.How likely is the merger?"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - afuturistic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters- served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.The move could be a step towards Musk's mission tobuild a self-sustaining city on Mars- a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.Figure caption,Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added."There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.What would it mean for customers?Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away fromless popular models.Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.Image source,NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption,Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the CyberTruck and Model 3Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said."The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, whichovertook Tesla as the world's biggest EV makerin January.What does Musk get out of it?The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said."The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.Elon Musk's stratospheric rise to trillionaire status - in chartsPublished13 JuneWho is Elon Musk and what is his net worth?Published12 JuneHowever, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Muskvalued around $1tn."I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.Related topicsInternational BusinessArtificial intelligenceElon MuskTeslaSpaceX

title: Elice's huge stock swings show AI's spending boom is getting more investor scrutiny
content:
The artificial intelligence boom may be entering a more unforgiving phase, as investors increasingly question whether the billions poured into data centers will translate into sustainable profits.

A bruising stock market debut by South Korean AI infrastructure provider Elice has become the latest warning sign that investors may be more closely scrutinizing ambitious expansion plans and paths to profitability.

Shares of the Seoul-based neocloud company plunged 32% in their trading debut Tuesday, even after it raised 201 billion won ($151 million) in an initial public offering priced at the top of its marketed range. The stock then rebounded by about 30% on Wednesday. Neoclouds offer specialized cloud infrastructure dedicated to AI workloads.

"This is a gut check moment in the tech trade," said Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives. "Investors are trying to better discern between the winners and losers and if there are any weak links in the tech AI food chain."

"Patience is wearing thin and scrutiny will be elevated especially for those taking on a major debt load like some of the neoclouds," he added.

The weak debut underscores a broader shift in sentiment toward the AI trade, where rising borrowing costs and concerns over debt-fueled expansion may force investors to distinguish between companies generating cash from the boom and those spending heavily in anticipation of future demand.

"The AI trade has moved from a phase where the size of the capex announcement was itself viewed positively to one where investors are asking who can actually earn an adequate return on that capital," said Billy Leung of Global X ETFs. "The market is distinguishing between companies that need capital to survive the build-out and companies that are being paid as the build-out continues."

The most vulnerable companies are neocloud providers expanding faster than their ability to generate cash, particularly those heavily dependent on external financing, according to Leung.

CoreWeave, one of the largest neocloud providers, is "the poster child of this whole thing," according to John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research. "This is broad market stress, not just speculation," he said, pointing to widening credit spreads.

Companies borrowing heavily to build computing capacity could face a squeeze if financing costs rise faster than revenue, particularly where construction expenses and depreciation mount before facilities reach full utilization.

The shift is particularly significant for Asia, where technology markets are heavily exposed to the semiconductor and memory-chip industries that have powered the global AI investment frenzy.

"U.S. semiconductor and AI plays are overbuilt. And in South Korea, even more overbuilt," Blank said.

South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics have been among the biggest beneficiaries of soaring demand for advanced memory chips, but their shares have come under pressure as investors reassess the sustainability of AI spending.

"Asia is simply much more directly geared to the hardware and memory side of the AI trade, so when investors question AI capex and financing, Korea and other North Asian technology markets feel it disproportionately," Leung said.

He added that rising earnings estimates across South Korea and Taiwan suggest the recent selloff reflects deteriorating sentiment and shrinking valuations rather than a sudden collapse in demand.

The change reflects a growing divide between companies with the financial firepower to sustain aggressive AI investments and those relying heavily on borrowing to fund expansion.

HSBC Chief Executive Officer Georges Elhedery warned that investors and lenders must become more discerning about which data-center projects deserve financing.

"You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements," he said. "You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."
