title: Hurricane Trudy makes its way toward Mexico as Typhoon Champi threatens Guam
content:
Hurricane Trudy moved toward the southwestern and west-central areas of Mexico's Pacific coast and could keep growing through Saturday, forecasters said.

Trudy's center will approach the coast on Saturday and pass near it into Sunday. A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo, Colima, to Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco.

The storm was a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph (150 kph) on Friday night.

Trudy was about 240 miles (385 kilometers) west-southwest of Acapulco, in the Mexican state of Guerrero, and about 215 miles (345 kilometers) south-southeast of Manzanillo, Colima state, while moving northwest at 8 mph (13 kph), the U.S. National Hurricane Center said.

The Mexican navy urged the maritime community and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution due to high waves, heavy rains and the risk of rising river levels, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.

The state of Colima said risks are currently low, but the storm could bring significant rainfall that could cause damage because the ground is saturated after successive storms have hit the Pacific coast.

Through the weekend, Trudy is expected to produce 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 cm) of rain, with isolated higher totals around 15 inches.

Also in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi was intensifying and moving west toward Guam at 15 mph (23 kph), with maximum sustained winds increasing to 100 mph (160 kph), according to the U.S. Weather Service and the U.S. Navy's Meteorology and Oceanography Command website.

A typhoon warning was issued for Guam and Rota, along with a tropical storm warning for Tinian, Saipan, and nearby areas.

title: Bending Spoons wants to revive software castoffs. Berkshire is backing the plan
content:
At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July,Bending Spoonswas a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote.

Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet:Berkshire Hathaway.

Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stakedisclosedon Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.

"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.

The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software providerAirtablefor about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending SpoonssaidMonday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.

For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. WithAnthropicandOpenAImarching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the "SaaSpocalypse."

Shares ofIntuit,HubSpotandAdobeare all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendorMiro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.

"You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore."

Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPOprospectus.

Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning withEvernotein 2022, followed byBrightcovein 2024, andVimeo,AOLandEventbritein 2025.

The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07.

Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade wereprivate equitybehemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.

Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions.

Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied."

"They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020.

Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years."

As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.

"Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now."

Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach.

"I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change."

For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow.

In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoonsliftedthe annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the companychangedits offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan.

"My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring toMicrosoft'snotetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote.

"They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost."

Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday.

"There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said.

For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven.

The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its firstearnings reportas a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million.

That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software.

On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise.

Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff.

"Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."

—CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

title: IMFC chair says global economy resilient; delegates walk out on Russian official
content:
The global economy is showing remarkable resilience but there is no room for complacency, the head of theInternational Monetary Fund'ssteering committee said on Saturday, while divisions overRussia'songoing war againstUkrainesparked a walkout of delegates.

SaudiFinance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who heads the IMF's steering committee, acknowledged the walkout by nearly half of delegates during remarks by Russia's finance minister at a meeting on Saturday, but said the important thing was that members ultimately agreed to the chair's statement.

"We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that's what matters," the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee told Reuters.

Al-Jadaan told a news conference that the global economy was demonstrating "remarkable resilience" in the face of profound ongoing challenges, including wars, threats to energy and food security, high public debt levels, and risks linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, while warning finance officials against letting down their guard.

"The message from the IMFC members is clear: there is no room for complacency," Al-Jadaan said in the final news conference of a week of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that brought more than 18,000 people to Bangkok.

"Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security," the chair's statement said.

Fiscal authorities should work to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable populations and growth-enhancing investments, Al-Jadaan told reporters, underscoring the need for continued central bank independence and policies that supported private sector-led growth and investment.

"International cooperation remains critical to addressing excessive global imbalances and trade tensions," he said.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called the meetings productive but said there was clearly heightened anxiety among members about increasing divergence.

Many lower-income countries that were not part of the AI value chain feared they were falling behind, she said.

"These meetings also have shown that in a world of repetitive shocks and geopolitical fragmentation, still there is desire for multilateral dialogue and cooperation," she said. "It is there."

Those comments came shortly after many IMFC delegates left the room when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel told a bank event on the sidelines of the meetings that nearly 50% of delegates took part in the walkout, sending a clear message to Russia.

"This is a very strong signal about solidarity and values. It would be the best for the world economy if this unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine would end," Nagel said. "I was really proud so many left this plenary."

The Bank of England confirmed that Governor Andrew Bailey was among the delegates who joined the walkout, which comes ahead of Britain hosting the G20 next year.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has roiled the IMFC, preventing it from reaching consensus statements in the years since. There were deep divisions again at this week's meetings as freshtensions flared between the US and Ukraine.

Sources said those who left while Siluanov spoke included delegates from Britain, Germany, France, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, among others.

"The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe," one European diplomat said. "We cannot normalize relations with Russia."

Germanyon Thursday warned against ​efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage after Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers, just over a month after the US hosted his first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.

US Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne told Reuters the same day that Washington, the current leader of the G20 nations, supported Russia's presence despite European concerns.

"We think it's really important if you're going to solve a crisis, you need to have open dialogue and open conversation," she told Reuters. "And you can't ​have ... dialogue, and you can't have resolution to conflict if no one's talking to one another."

Ukraine's finance minister participated virtually in the meetings, in order to focus on budget priorities at home.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking at a European Union summit on Friday, blasted US President Donald Trump'sdiesel dealwith Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in peace talks.

EU leaders have rallied around Zelenskyy after Trump again criticized Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace." Trump on Fridaywaiveda new congressional requirement to impose harsh sanctions on Russia.

title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act, citing national interest
content:
PresidentDonald Trumpsigned an executive order late Friday waiving parts of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine.

"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver isin the national interestsof the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order.

The House passed theRussia sanctions billon Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the lateLindsey Graham, a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina.

Titled theLindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continuedfull-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries includingChinaandIndiathat are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas.

Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders.

The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran.

Oil sales revenue iscritical to fundingRussia's war effort.

The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarilywaived sanctionson Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran.

High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.

"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian PresidentVladimir Putin'seconomy envoy, said in aposton X.

"The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added.

But Trump's opponents have criticized the move.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver.

"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthalsaidin an X post.

Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyywarned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.

"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."

Earlier this week, reports emerged thatUkraine has restricted SpaceX'sStarlink military application, Starshield.SpaceXCEOElon Musksaid in a post on X that the U.S. government and presidentwereultimately responsiblefor any curbs on the network.

title: Trump's Russia diesel deal may offer Putin more than money — and spell trouble for Ukraine
content:
Ukraine is facing increasing uncertainty over its ability to sustain the war against Russia as a series of moves by U.S. PresidentDonald Trumphas raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.

Trump's agreement with Putin toease sanctions for Russiato provide global markets with diesel, as well as restrictions on U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukrainian forces, has put PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyin a difficult position aswinter looms.

Higher diesel prices – essential to transporting goods and agricultural production – tend todrive up costsacross the wider economy and fuel inflation. With November's U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump is under pressure to bring fuel costs down.

But experts told CNBC that the diesel deal would deliver only a marginal financial benefit to Russia, and not move the needle much on global energy prices. Its wider political implications may be more significant, potentially reinforcing the Kremlin's belief that it can secure concessions from Washington without making compromises over Ukraine.

"Russia's main gain is political: Trump's decision eases sanctions pressure and undermines Western unity," Sergey Aleksashenko, senior research fellow and head of economics at the NEST Centre, told CNBC.

Trump's agreement with Putin was for Russia to supply the global market with 4.8 million metric tons of diesel, the equivalent of aboutten days of U.S. domestic demand, or about a single day of global demand. Experts say it will do little to affect prices.

"It does not even touch the sides – it is very, very small," Neil Atkinson, former head of the IEA's oil industry and markets division, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.

Aleksashenko estimated that the initial part of the phased agreement that covers 1.8 million metric tons of diesel could generate up to $1.25 billion in additional export revenue over three months, equivalent to around 1% of Russia's commodity export revenues during that period.

However, the benefit to Russia's federal budget would be substantially smaller, at less than $30 million per month, or under 0.07% of monthly federal revenues.

The deal was therefore unlikely to meaningfully strengthen Russia's war finances, Aleksashenko said. Instead, its main benefit to Moscow is political, because it eased sanctions pressure and undermined Western unity without requiring Putin to make concessions over Ukraine, he told CNBC.

The research fellow also argued that the additional Russian diesel entering global markets is not sufficient to produce a noticeable reduction in consumer fuel prices in the short term.

"Funding the war is currently Putin's priority, and he is prepared to increase that funding even if it means cutting all other expenditures," Aleksashenko added, pointing to Russia's draft budget for 2027.

"Rather than encouraging compromise, the [diesel] deal likely boosts Moscow's belief that continued pressure will eventually yield further Western concessions," Maria Snegovaya, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.

Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy also warned that the diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.

"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."

Earlier this week, reports emerged thatSpaceX'sStarlink military application Starshield has been restricted in Ukraine. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and presidentwereultimately responsiblefor any curbs on the network.

The order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House,according to a Reuters reportciting three officials familiar with the matter. CNBC has contacted the White House for comment.

The consequences were felt sharply in Ukraine. As Starlink's speed limits were lowered, Ukraine became incapable of shooting down some Russian drones. This week, Ukraine also did not receive advanced warning from partners of incoming ballistic missiles, resulting in civilian deaths, according to Ukrainian officials.

According to Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport,Starlink restrictions emboldened Russiato intensify attacks on Ukraine.

"With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach told CNBC on Friday.

Russian authorities didn't respond to multiple CNBC requests for comment.

The diesel deal was a political and moral blow to Ukraine and the Western coalition, according to Snegovaya. The U.S. sanctions exemption, which runs until April 2027, could facilitate Russian diesel exports beyond the initially announced shipment, potentially increasing Moscow's economic gains, she warned.

"If [the] White House uses its military and intelligence support as leverage to constrain Ukraine's strikes, the implications could become far more significant," Snegovaya said, adding that Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries have inflicted substantial economic costs on Moscow.

Such a move could have far greater consequences for Ukraine's efforts to weaken Russia's war economy, she added.

The diesel deal further undermines Washington's credibility as a mediator in the eyes of Ukraine and its European allies, as it appears to reward Moscow without securing concessions while increasing pressure on Kyiv, she said.

The problem, Snegovaya said, is that achieving military autonomy for Europe and Ukraine is extremely difficult in the short term, and Europe has been slow to develop the necessary capabilities.

"Almost five years into the war, Ukraine and its European partners remain heavily dependent on the U.S. in critical areas, like intelligence and missile defense. These dependencies are unlikely to be overcome during the remaining years of the Trump administration," she told CNBC.

title: Some companies give AI to everyone. This CEO is doing the opposite
content:
At London-headquartered payments technology company Paysend, access to artificial intelligence tools has to be earned.CEO Ben Chisell told CNBC he is a “very cynical man” about the hype around the technology, though he still sees value in it.

Chisell, who previously worked at Amazon, eBay and Starling Bank, estimates that Paysend can now deliver around 25% more engineering work with the same-sized team, but argues that getting results isn’t as simple as handing everyone the latest tech.

Instead, he limits AI tools to his highest-performing employees, often only after they’ve proved what they can do with them. In the wrong hands, he said, AI can magnify bad habits such as laziness and poor judgment.

His broader rule is to resist the “fear of missing out” and focus on customer problems.

“I know it sounds very unglamorous and unsexy as an approach given the world of tokenmaxxing and AI, but I think it’s really, really important,” Chisell said.

The pressure to demonstrate AI’s value is growing, from thelegal sectorto software engineering and finance, and many companies are responding by putting the technology in as many hands as possible.

London-based Lloyds Banking Group has rolled out 40,000 Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, with 97% of employees who have one actively using it, the bank said. Newcastle-headquartered software company Sage said its AI coding tools had saved hundreds of thousands of work hours, while London-based professional services firm Grant Thornton UK has encouraged all of its staff to use Anthropic’s Claude as part of a £500 million ($660 million) investment in AI.

These figures do not necessarily translate into gains on the bottom line, however. U.K. governmentresearchpublished in January found that three-quarters of businesses using AI said it had improved workforce productivity, but 77% said revenue had not changed.

Like Chisell, Lokdeep Singh, CEO of British enterprise software company Unily, sees AI as a “superpower” best reserved for high-performing employees. He is also wary of companies giving it out to everyone as a way to reduce costs.

“I personally believe you should use it to expand your ambition rather than make the team smaller,” he told CNBC. “But the reality is that in many industries, again, because of the macro environment, it is being thought as: ‘OK, can I cut costs? Can I cut employees?’ The truth is probably somewhere in between.”

At Paysend, Chisell wants employees to demonstrate what a tool actually contributes. New hires get a month to experiment with AI tools and explain what they have achieved.

He recently put that policy to the test with a new search engine optimization lead who requested access to Claude. A month later, the employee told Chisell he no longer needed it. All he found it useful for, he said, was producing briefs more quickly. So instead of a general-purpose AI tool, the employee suggested building a dedicated content-brief agent, which he is now working on.

At software company CoreView, the approach has been different. London-based CEO Simon Azzopardi told CNBC the company was initially “very gung-ho” on AI, initiating a widespread rollout for its software engineers. They first used AI to investigate problems by correlating logs, events and data, as well as to produce technical documentation and onboard new engineers faster.

Now, he said, developers increasingly coordinate teams of AI agents handling tasks including back-end and front-end coding, quality assurance and documentation. Azzopardi said work that previously took weeks could now take days.

However, AI-generated work isn’t necessarily productive if employees use it to build things outside their expertise, Azzopardi warned. “You feel more efficient, but you actually aren’t,” he said.

Still, when onboarding a major customer in the U.K.’s National Health Service, CoreView only needed to add one engineer while continuing to deliver its other projects, he said. The company has been hiring rather than cutting staff, using the extra capacity to take on more work.

As AI takes on more of people’s existing responsibilities, the question is what happens to the employees who used to do these tasks. Chisell believes companies will thrive if they help employees move into new roles, rather than replace them once their work is automated.

Customer-service workers, for example, have spent years resolving complex issues — a skill that’s valuable across a business, he said. For Chisell, technology should never replace human responsibility.

“Having a human in the loop shouldn’t mean human CC’d,” he said. “It should mean human ownership.”

title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
content: Image caption,British Airways planes lined up at Terminal 5 at Heathrow AirportByFaisal Islam,ÂEconomics editorÂandÂTabby WilsonPublished17 October 2026Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department."We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".Asked about the project in September, Burnhamsuggested it was an argument for London to decide."I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbyesaid it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners"."Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.The project, which has an estimated price tag of Â£33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has sincesuggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.Related topicsHeathrow Airport expansionJohn HealeyLondon Heathrow AirportMore on this storyNot building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow bossPublished4 days agoAndy Burnham refuses to back third runway at HeathrowPublished27 September

title: Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses
content: Image source,AFP via Getty ImagesByFaisal IslamEconomics EditorPublished17 October 2026When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the BudgetPublished3 days ago'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UKPublished8 OctoberThree things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMFPublished4 days agoBut there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs.It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump.But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.Related topicsUK economyEconomyInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)John HealeyEconomics

title: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
content:
The U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with abudget deficitof nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress.

The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, theTreasury Departmentreported Friday.

It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official.

With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its25th straight fiscal yearoperating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001.

Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the10-yearand30-yearU.S. Treasury yields to24-year highslast week.

Social Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025.

Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025.

Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion.

Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year.

In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owedexceeded $40 trillionearlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can"grow our way out of"its increasing debt pile.

"Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August.

PresidentDonald Trumppitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite theSupreme Court rulingearlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional.

The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due torefunds requiredfollowing the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers.

The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

title: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
content:
One of the last bigcampaign-financesnapshots before the Nov. 3Election Dayis now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats.

On one side,Democratic candidateshave turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds.

Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedentedflood of outside super PAC cash, bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led byTeslaandSpaceXCEOElon Musk. The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amidstubbornly high inflationanddrooping approval ratingsfor President Donald Trump.

A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised andspentfrom July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings.

Here are CNBC's five takeaways:

If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves.

Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals.James Talaricoraised$60.2 millionin Texas,Jon Ossoffbrought in $33.1 million in Georgia andAbdul El-Sayedraised $30.7 million in Michigan.Sherrod Brownbrought in $23.1 million in Ohio, whileTroy Jacksonraised $20.4 million in Maine,Mary Peltola$14.1 million in Alaska andRoy Cooper$12.2 million in North Carolina.

Even in reliably red Kansas, DemocratAdam Hamiltonraised$9.4 million.

In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close.Ken Paxtonraised about $10.2 million in Texas,Mike Rogers$9.7 million in Michigan,Susan Collins$5.2 million in Maine andJon Husted$4.8 million in Ohio.

Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it.

The same fundraising edge stretches into the House.

Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, DemocratJamie Agerraised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for RepublicanJennifer Balkcom.

The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: theCook Political Report with Amy Walterprojected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber.

While Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending.

TheSenate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, theCongressional Leadership Fundraised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing.

That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled$158 millioninto Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings.

Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska,The Wall Street Journalreported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 millionbacking Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.

The blitz allowed Republicans to hold anaired-ad advantagein seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact.

But polls have shownlittle movementin recent weeks, despite the advantage.

No donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.

He pumped more than$276 millioninto federal political groups during the third quarter, making him thebiggest known individual donorof the midterms. His disclosed giving included$158 millionto Senate Leadership Fund and another $89 million to hisAmerica PAC, according to FEC filings.

Most of that capital was earmarked for a single rescue mission: Texas, the state that's his primary residence and headquarters of his businesses.

Musk gave the SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23. Both times, the SLF transferred the exact same amount toTexas PACthe following day. The group, which is backing Paxton, reported no other donors through the end of September.

Until now, many national Republicans had beenreluctantto sink resources into the Lone Star state's expensive media market while fighting across an already expanded Senate map. Musk effectively erased that trade-off, supplying enough money to build a dedicated financial firewall around Paxton without forcing the party to pull resources from other battlegrounds.

For months, Democrats worried over the reluctance oftraditional megadonorsto write checks following the 2024 election cycle with presidential contest drama at the top of the ticket. The latest filings suggest that freeze is thawing — though much money is still bypassing the Democratic National Committee.

Facebookco-founderDustin Moskovitzand his wife,Cari Tuna, put about $16 million into the midterm fight this summer, according to FEC filings, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who had also withheld money from the DNC this cycle, poured $11.5 million into the super PAC backing Talarico earlier this year.

The renewed megadonor money gives Democrats another source of firepower for the final weeks that can be quickly redirected if needed.

Already,Democrats' Senate Majority PACraised a record $151 million in the third quarter and ended September with $112 million in cash, even as its Republican counterpart raised substantially more.

All the spending is feeding an election on track to shatter spending records.

AdImpact projects$11.6 billion in political advertising during the 2025-26 election cycle, which would make 2026 the most expensive cycle on record — surpassing both the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms and the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential cycle.

The congressional fight alone has already put$3.8 billion in advertisingon the air, more than $870 million ahead of the comparable point in 2024, according to AdImpact. Senate races are helping drive the surge: the firm projects $3.4 billion in Senate advertising by the end of the cycle, up 48% from 2022.

But as the amount of money rises, some of it is becoming harder for voters to trace back to its original source.

Thursday's filings showed millions flowing into super PACs from nonprofits and other entities that are not required to disclose their own donors, leaving the original source of some of the cycle's biggest checks hidden.

title: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
content:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.

Brentfutures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%.

U.S.West Texas Intermediaterose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.

Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, amilitary spokesmansaid. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.

Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. One of Aramco's administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit on Tuesday, the kingdom'senergy ministry said. The militants attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300.

In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have comeunder attacksince Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday,U.S. Central Commandsaid. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority.

The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to theInternational Maritime Organization.

Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler.

Meanwhile, the "energy ceasefire" that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continuedattacking Ukrainian infrastructuredespite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv wouldresume strikeson Russian refineries in retaliation.

Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data.

U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

title: Debt is eating up a bigger chunk of your raise, research shows
content:
A version of this article first appeared in ″CNBC's Money 101 Newsletter with Sharon Epperson,″ an eight-week series with monthly updates to help improve your financial well-being.Subscribe nowto receive the series in your inbox. It is alsoavailable in Spanish.

Consumer spendinghas helped keep the U.S. economy resilient. Yet research showsdebt paymentsare taking a growing bite out of Americans' income gains, leaving less money available to spend or save.

Anew analysisby the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation and the consumer advocacy group Protect Borrowers found that a typical U.S. household's estimated real take-home monthly pay rose $109 from late 2022 to early 2026. "Real" take-home pay is one's wage after accounting for inflation.

Meanwhile, a worker's monthly debt payments rose $57.

In other words, researchers estimate that for a one-earner household, 52 cents of every dollar of income gained in recent years goes to higher debt payments. For a two-earner household, they project that the entire real income gain, and then some, goes toward debt.

The analysis also found inflation-adjusted debt payments rose nearly 15% over roughly three years — about eight times as fast as household income, which grew less than 2%.

The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers analyzed credit records for millions of working-age Americans ages 25 to 64, along with Census Bureau income data.The research includes payments on credit cards,auto loansand leases,student loansand home equity lines of credit. It excludesmortgagesand some other borrowing, including manybuy now, pay later loansand medical payment plans.

Angela Hanks, chief of policy programs at The Century Foundation, said the findings may understate the financial pressure households face.

"Even though it shows that workers' wages are getting eaten up by debt payments at a tremendous level," Hanks said, the findings represent "perhaps the rosiest analysis that we could have done using the data."

She said adding mortgage payments as well as installment loans not included in a credit file — like buy now, pay later and payday loans — would have made household debt payments higher.

Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead.

More consumers are relying on credit cards tocover basic expenseswhen their paychecks fall short, she said.

Separate Federal Reserve data underscores the strain. The Fed's latestSurvey of Consumer Financesfound 8.6% of families spent more than 40% of their income on debt payments in 2025, up from 6.5% in 2022 — a level not seen since the 2013 survey.

Mortgages and student loans are often considered"good debt"because they may help build wealth or earning power. But even potentially beneficial debt, or debt taken on for necessary expenses, can become a financial burden.

"When that debt stretches out for six months or a year or longer, or if you're taking out a seven-year auto loan, or if you're taking out a longer mortgage than maybe you ideally would want to, or a bigger mortgage, that's when things get a little dicey," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More."

To avoid taking on more debt than you can afford, he recommends three simple steps:

Before taking on debt, consider the total borrowing cost, repayment terms and whether you have enough savings to handle unexpected expenses, Schulz said.

— CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting.

title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
content:
New White House press secretaryKatie Zachariais leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over herperformance, a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday.

Earlier Friday afternoon, PresidentDonald Trumptold reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit.

"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House.

"'If I were you, I'd reconsider,' " the president said he told Zacharia.

The White House official, who spoke condition of anonymity to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role.

Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly.

By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci.

"Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked atTrump Media & Technology Group, had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background.

Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.

But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.

In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to GreeceKimberly Guilfoylehad been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow a number ofother high-ranking female officialsin the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months.

"You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House.

He accused the media of treating her "very badly," and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night.

Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney."

Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied.

Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day.

"She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'"

Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
content:
President Donald Trumpon Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week onStarlink satellite internetservices provided to Ukraine's armed forces.

Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday saidSpaceXhad restricted use ofStarshield, a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.

SpaceX CEOElon Muskpinnedresponsibility for any restrictionson the U.S. government and Trump,writingon X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."

Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military.

"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."

Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in apost on Telegramthis week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions."

Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX.

"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" hewrote. "As your European customers, we are watching you."

Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.

The Telegraphreported Fridaythat Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.

On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."

Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.

SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

title: Wall Street's fear gauge is ripping. Traders see it going even higher
content:
The sell-off in AI-related stocks pushed theCboe Volatility Index (VIX)above 22 for the first time in four months. A cluster of trades suggests it could go even higher.

In a series of eyebrow raising trades, investors purchased a number of November VIX calls that payoff if the index stays elevated through November. Specifically, one trader bought 9200 of the November 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million and 12,500 of the November 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million, wagering that the VIX will close above 23 by the third week of November.

"The speed at which VIX increased today, combined with elevated VIX options volume suggests traders are actively monetizing October VIX positions and rolling to hedge a larger market downturn. We note several +$1 million call VIX prints for November," said Brent Kochuba, founder of SpotGamma and a CNBC contributor.

Cracks in the AI complex and fears around neo-cloud provider CoreWeave caused the Nasdaq to shed 2%, its worst day since June 5th. CoreWeave lost 13%.

Of the top ten most popular VIX contracts to buy in Friday's session, nine were calls, and six were at strikes above where the VIX fell to after its initial spike. Nearly $27M in premium was traded across those nine contracts, or just about 36% of the total premium traded in VIX options on the day.

The market faces a key test next week when Tesla, SpaceX and Meta report earnings.

title: What happens after bankruptcy? A debt attorney explains what comes next
content:
Filing for bankruptcycan feel like the end of a long, exhausting process, but it's also the start of a new financial chapter. Once you've filed, you may have questions about how bankruptcy affectsyour creditand what steps you can take to move forward.

CNBC Selectspoke withLeslie Tayne, a debt relief attorney, about what to expect after filing, which financial mistakes to avoid and how to start rebuilding your credit.

After a bankruptcy discharge, qualifying debts are legally cleared, meaning you're generally no longer personally responsible for paying them. However, not all debts qualify, and certain liens may remain. In Chapter 7, a discharge typically comes a few months after filing; in Chapter 13, it generally follows completion of the repayment plan.

Bankruptcy also remains on yourcredit reportfor up to 10 years from filing for Chapter 7 and seven years for Chapter 13.It can lower your credit scoreand make it harder to qualify for credit cards, car loans or a mortgage, or mean paying higher interest rates. The impact varies, but bankruptcy doesn't prevent you from obtaining credit forever. With time and responsible financial habits, you can begin rebuilding your credit and expanding your options.

Offers in this section are from affiliate partners and selected based on a combination of engagement, product relevance, compensation, and consistent availability.

Credit Saint offers a 90-day money-back guarantee and has received an A rating from the Better Business Bureau.

The Credit People's Credit Report Repair service is more affordable than many competitors and even the standard package includes unlimited challenges to all three credit bureaus. The premium package includes escalated disputes and monthly credit score reports.

"The first year after filing for bankruptcy should be about prioritizing financial stability," Tayne says. That means adjusting to a budget, rebuilding savings and learning to manage credit responsibly, including "unlearning financial habits that didn't serve you." Because qualifying for new credit may be more difficult at first, she recommends focusing on paying bills on time, keeping spending manageable and avoiding unnecessary new debt.

"The first year can be financially disheartening, but bankruptcy provides a fresh start," she says. "Just keep in mind that recovery takes time, and stay the course."

It's also important to know that bankruptcy doesn't eliminate every debt. "Some debts simply aren't dischargeable or can survive bankruptcy," Tayne says, pointing tostudent loansand certain tax debts as examples. Whether these obligations can be discharged depends on the circumstances and applicable legal requirements. Talk with your bankruptcy attorney about which debts will be cleared and which you'll still need to repay.

Taking on new debt before you're financially ready is one of the biggest mistakes to avoid, says Tayne. Many people receive new credit offers after filing for bankruptcy and may be tempted to start spending again before they've established a stable financial foundation. Instead, focus on managing expenses, building an emergency fund and ensuring that any new credit is affordable.

For some people, getting back on track may also mean reducing major expenses, such as housing costs. Moving somewhere with lower rent can free up money each month, although it's important to weigh potential savings against moving costs and other practical considerations.

If overspending contributed to the original debt, developing healthier financial habits can help prevent future financial problems. However, bankruptcy can result from many circumstances, including job loss, medical bills or other unexpected expenses. As Tayne points out, shame and avoidance can make it harder to ask for help, but reaching out to areputable financial counseloror other qualified professional can be an important step toward rebuilding financial stability.

Rebuilding your credit after bankruptcy takes time, but consistent financial habits can help you make progress.

Pay your bills on time.Start by keeping up with bills and financial obligations that remain payable after bankruptcy. "It takes savvy budgeting and perseverance," Tayne says. You may need to adjust your living expenses to make room for essential payments and avoid falling behind.

These payments typically aren't included in traditional credit scoring, but adding them could help improve your score. Experian Boost won't erase the impact of bankruptcy, and results vary: some users see their scores increase, while others may not see a change.

Do the math before taking on new debt.Whether you're considering a new credit card or a loan, make sure the payments fit your budget before committing. Consider the interest rate, fees and total repayment cost, too. Building a realistic budget and sticking to it can help you manage future borrowing responsibly, Tayne says.

Understand how Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 can affect your recovery.Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy follow different processes, which can affect how people rebuild their finances. "Chapter 13 usually involves a repayment plan, which can take three to five years, and that alone is draining," Tayne says. Ultimately, your financial recovery depends on several factors, including your income, essential expenses, payment history and how consistently you manage your budget moving forward.

"It's so common for consumers to think that once they file for bankruptcy, their finances will never get back in order, or that it's an easy way out," Tayne says. "This isn't true."

In her 25 years as a debt attorney, Tayne says she's seen many clients file for bankruptcy and go on to achieve financial success. But rebuilding takes time. "It's not a wipe and go but a rebuilding process. It takes discipline and commitment," she says.

Take things one step at a time. Focus on managing your expenses, paying your bills on time and avoiding new debt you can't afford. With patience and consistent financial habits, you can work toward a more stable financial future.

title: NBA tightens betting rules, develops AI to flag suspicious wagers
content:
The NBA is upping the ante when it comes to monitoring sports betting ahead of the 2026-2027 season.

The league is tightening restrictions on bets offered by its authorized gambling partners and deploying artificial intelligence to help identify suspicious wagering, according to two documents obtained by CNBC.

The measures come as Commissioner Adam Silver pushes for greater access to wagering data and more control over the types of markets offered on the league's games. He said his concerns extend to prediction markets.

"For us, whether it's called a prediction market, whether it's sports betting, it's the same issues for our league, and I think for all the leagues," Silver told CNBC last week in Macao. "There's issues around integrity first and foremost."

In the letter sent to sports betting companies includingFanDuel,DraftKings, Fanatics and others, the NBA has placed restrictions on wagers on which player scores the first basket, wagers on players expected to play less than 12 minutes per game and parlays combining multiple bets on the same player's underperformance.

Those types of bets can raise integrity concerns because a single player has the ability to influence the outcome.

The changes follow a series of gambling-related cases involving NBA figures including former players Jontay Porter, Terry Rozier, and Damon Jones and former coach and player Chauncey Billups.

A separate memo sent Friday to team presidents, general managers, integrity officers and lawyers says the NBA has developed an internal AI-based monitoring platform. The system analyzes basketball data, injury reports, social media information about player availability and individual betting data.

The platform is designed to help the league “promptly identify and investigate potentially suspicious betting activity,” according to the memo from Dan Spillane, the NBA’s executive vice president of league governance and policy.

Silver’s comments underscore the importance the league places on obtaining that information.

“So we want access to that data. We also want control over the markets,” Silver told CNBC.

The league is also increasing its training and education around sports betting. The memo said that former NFL player and retired FBI agent Charles Tillman, will provide in-person training to each team.

The league said it has also added new training around sports betting to NBA rookies who will now receive training at the NBA Combine and during the required Rookie Transition program.

The letter also highlights steps the league is taking to better protect players and personnel from harassment and threats by sports bettors.

As betting has become more widespread, some bettors have taken to social media to harass players for their game performance that may be tied to a bet.

To address this, the league has updated its NBA Fan Code of Conduct to highlight the prohibition on betting-related harassment.

The league is also partnering with a third-party service provider to help monitor and control harassing messages. It has also launched a new text message-based hotline to securely report threats.

The memo does not specify how the restrictions would apply to prediction market platforms.

In Macao, Silver said that he's in favor of a national framework when it comes to federal regulation around sports betting.

"We have roughly 40 different judications regulating us right now so to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest," he said.

title: S&P 500 dragged down by AI stocks as chip shares head for worst week since July: Live updates

Other areas of the market such as financials saw gains.JPMorganadvanced around 2%. Additionally, shares of sporting goods retailerNikeand drugmakerMerckeach climbed around 1%, adding to the Dow's rise.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month.
