title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Google's translation service handles one trillion words per monthByJohn LaurensonBusiness reporter,ÂReporting fromParisPublished1 hour ago"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard."It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator."You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says FranÃ§ois Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs"."But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.In April, Google saidpeople are now translating,externalone trillion words a month with Google Translate.That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.Direct sales of machine translation,external(i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (Â£1bn) last year.Image source,John ZimmermanImage caption,AI translation is the "right call" in many cases says John Zimmerman"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages."For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI."Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.But that human input is required less and less."The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft."Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.Not yet, translators argue.Ariella BaltiÃ© is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them."There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says BaltiÃ©.When the AI saw "Madame X, Ã©pouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.Image source,Ariella BaltiÃ©Image caption,Ariella BaltiÃ© specialises in legal translation workAccuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field."The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter Î¼ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth)."That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult."Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."Image source,Carol BereuterImage caption,Carol Bereuter is a specialist in medical translations"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns FranÃ§ois Yvon.Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says."When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work."27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging."As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says FranÃ§ois Yvon.This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement."We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt."The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.Related topicsInternational BusinessTechnology of BusinessArtificial intelligenceMore on this storyThe critical tech staying safe by going undergroundPublished19 AugustTokenomics: Why making AI pay is trickyPublished12 AugustWhy airlines are warning over lithium-ion batteriesPublished7 August

title: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
content:
BEIJING — Equity investors are skeptical of Chinese companies' rapid expansion overseas, according to Goldman Sachs.

The "market wants to look for profitable expansions," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs Research,said on a podcastthat the investment bank published Tuesday.

Sluggish consumer demand in China has pushed many companies, such as electric car brands, toaccelerate plans for enteringother countries. Automaker Geely is one of the latest Chinese companies to push further abroad, announcing Friday it plans toenter Canada next year.

Chinese companies' overseas market share will likely reach 31% by 2035, up from around 18%, Chen and her team predicted in a Sept. 14 report. Their analysis covered more than 10 sectors, including express delivery, industrial robots and so-called white goods such as air conditioners.

Chinese businesses often find higher profit margins abroad than they would at home, enabling the companies to charge lower prices than local competitors.

Investors need to be convinced the global expansion "does not end up with something similar to involution, where the price actually gets killed because of competition," Chen said Tuesday, adding that geopolitics and market access restrictions also weighs on stock performance.

Involution refers to race-to-the-bottom competition in China, which regulators have attempted to address in recent years.

That uncertainty means Chinese companies have very little of their global expansion opportunity priced into their stocks, Chen said.

But on the flip side, she noted that investors are "ruthless" when incumbent companies lose their market share: A 10% to 15% loss could shrink market capitalization by 50% to 80%.

The Chinese players are not just looking at the U.S. and Europe. Goldman Sachs noted some of the most rapid growth is in emerging markets, as the businesses also pursue areas underserved by competitors.

"Chinese brands are no longer simply market challengers," Euromonitor said in a report last month. "Brands are becoming long-term, embedded competitors capable ofreshaping market dynamicsacross Latin America.

title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?
content: Figure caption,Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?ByDaniel ThomasÂandÂOliver Smith,ÂBBC NewsPublished1 hour agoWould you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications,graduates,externaland recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI."Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."Image source,SuppliedImage caption,Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicantsWhile Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI whensome are using it themselves to screen candidates."That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."'More competition for students'This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process".According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.'It's not a level playing field'Image source,EDFImage caption,EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employeesHollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process."What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills.But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews."A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff'Published25 March 2025AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analystsPublished5 MarchYoung jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AIPublished21 MayOne recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would."I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving.EDF does not currently use AI screening but Hollie Moody says they may have to in future.She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits."It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."Related topicsEmploymentArtificial intelligenceEDF Energy

title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByColletta Smith,ÂBBC Your Voice correspondentÂandÂElaine Doran,ÂBBC Your Voice producerPublished1 hour agoAbout 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class."I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobsPublished6 days agoOnly three-quarters of first class mail delivered on timePublished29 MayRoyal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff sayPublished16 FebruarySome postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload.We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day.Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare"."We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands.Image caption,Bryn Dymott says he is speaking out now because he wants people to know what's really happeningBryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas."People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered."Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening.He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise."'A boat taking on water'So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices.Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems.The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others."Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU.The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing.Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas.It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses."The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period.Image caption,The BBC saw returned post that couldn't be delivered so ended up back on the frames in a Royal Mail officeRoyal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans tocut 2,500 head office and other supporting rolesby the end of 2027.The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out.The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than Â£37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday."We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire."We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working."An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us."Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance."

title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, D.C. to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
content:
Anthropicis asking a federal court in Washington, D.C. to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models.

"The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation."

The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic'sClaude AI models.

Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on itsClaude modelswas arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.

Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety."

Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a$200 millioncontract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD'sGenAI.milAI platform that September, talks collapsed.

A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. The Pentagon didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this report.

title: Here's where Jim Cramer stands on this newly public AI infrastructure stock
content:
There's a new picks-and-shovels play on the artificial intelligence build-out, but CNBC'sJim Cramersaid Tuesday that investors should keep the stock at arm's length.

The "Mad Money" host gave two primary reasons for holding off onAccelevation Holdings: He's becoming more cautious about data center stocks ahead of the midterm elections and prefers established companies with proven track records. That's why Cramer'sCharitable Trust, the portfolio run by the CNBC Investing Club, instead owns shares of AI infrastructure players such as gas turbine makerGE Vernovaand electrical equipment supplierEaton.

"Accelevation has an exciting story, but after it came public with a whimper, I'm not too eager to jump on this one," he said. "For now, I say let's put Accelevation on our watch list and see if management can deliver before we pull the trigger."

Accelevation, which makes and installs electric, cooling equipment and support structures inside data centers, priced its offering on Sept. 29 at $18 per share, below its proposed offering range. Shares debuted the next day and closed at $17.95. They have since fallen to just over $15, a disappointing first couple of weeks for a company benefiting from surging demand for AI infrastructure.

Cramer's first concern extends beyond Accelevation. With the midterm elections just three weeks away, he expectspolitical opposition to data center constructionto remain a headwind for the broader industry. The enormous electricity demands of these facilities and their potential impact on energy costs have becomepolitical flashpoints, making Cramer reluctant to recommend buying into the sector before voters head to the polls.

"If you're going to buy a data center supplier, I think you should wait three weeks until after the election — that's when I expect some of the political heat to die down," he said.

His second concern is specific to Accelevation. While the company's growth has been impressive, Cramer is less confident in its ability to consistently turn that demand into profits, particularly as it competes with larger industrial players.

Accelevation's revenue surged 147% in 2025, while sales jumped another 176% year over year in the first half of 2026. However, higher labor costs and project inefficiencies weighed on gross margins during that period. "That tells me some of this work has been much harder to execute profitably than these guys expected," Cramer said.

He also expressed concerns about Accelevation's competitive position, citingVertivand Eaton as established companies that pursue overlapping segments of the data center infrastructure market. "There are a ton of different ways to play this story," he said. "I'd rather go with the ones that have earned my confidence."

title: Saudi national charged with secretly planting recording device in OpenAI office
content: Image source,US Department of JusticeImage caption,Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorderByMax MatzaPublished13 October 2026, 22:19 BSTUpdated 4 minutes agoA Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".Image source,US Department of JusticeImage caption,The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paperOn 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (Â£187,000).This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. Please refresh the page for the fullest version.You can receive Breaking News on a smartphone or tablet via theBBC News App. You can also follow@BBCBreaking on X,externalto get the latest alerts.Related topicsArtificial intelligenceUnited States

title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI employee who allegedly planted recording device in conference room
content:
AnOpenAIemployee was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday.

The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated.

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology."

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance."

Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before it was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room. The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted.

The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room.

This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors likeAnthropicand other big tech names, facesheightened scrutinyover safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems.

Last week, OpenAIdefended its decisionto fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."

Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI."

title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove lobe of lung, Vatican says
content:
Pope Leo was diagnosed with a common form of lung cancer after doctors removed a lower lobe of his right lung in surgery on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.

The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.

The pope was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health checkup.

The Vatican had said earlier on Tuesday evening that the surgery had been successful before providing a more detailed update from the pope's lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, the chief of thoracic surgery at the Gemelli.

"In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," said Margaritora's update.

"A rapid intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as had been suspected from the pre-operative tests," it said.

Tuesday's surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room.

The statement did not provide further details.

Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1 p.m. (1100 GMT) in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9 km (5.6 miles) north of the Vatican to the Gemelli.

Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted 'Auguri' (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance.

The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to recover in hospital for about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until October 20.

Leo, elected by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.

The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, was hospitalized several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025.

Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17.

The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.

Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalized.

He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru.

Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that "We need you here (on Earth)," he said.

"I never looked back," said Leo.

title: Airport attacks put aviation in crosshairs of geopolitical conflicts
content:
Deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiestairportover the past week are highlighting howconflictsin the Middle East are upending air travel on a larger scale.

Aviation is increasingly in the middle of these sprawling clashes as threats and outright attacks have forced airlines to quicklycancel flightsthroughout the Middle East for days, weeks and, in some cases, months. Some carriers might redeploy planes that would be going to some Middle East destinations like Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Doha, Qatar, to other locations altogether.

"It's a new paradigm. Civil aviation is being directly targeted and it has not been the case in the last couple of decades," said Mark Zee, founder of OpsGroup, an independent aviation safety group whose members include pilots, dispatchers, airline employees and others.

TheSaudi airport attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. Over the weekend, at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured when a projectile hit terminals at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials said. Other attacks have included drones.

"Historically, airport security is focused on preventing unauthorized access to aircraft and the airport, not defending airspace," said Jeff Price, a professor at the Metropolitan State University of Denver's Department of Aviation and Aerospace Science and an airport management consultant.

The threats to aviation are forcing officials to rethink how to protect blind spots in these major public spaces.

"There is this established way to deal with kind of more conventional weapons such as missiles. It's very expensive, but there is a way," said Gulnaz Ukassova, UAE-based security director of information and analysis at risk management firm International SOS. "There is still no sort of foolproof way to deal with the threat posed by drones. The technology, obviously, is constantly evolving."

King Khalid International Airport has been shut down for much of this week, and some carriers suspended operations there, citing safety concerns. CEOs of major oil companies also pulled out of an energy conference in the country.

Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, was less than two weeks away from launching anAtlanta-Riyadh route, the first nonstop commercial flight between the the two countries operated by a U.S. airline, according to the carrier.

But late Sunday, the Federal Aviation AdministrationwarnedU.S. carriers about safety-of-flight risks when flying in or over Saudi Arabia. On Monday morning, Delta said it would postpone the route's debut until March.

The new Delta route comes as Saudi leadership seeks to boost tourism to the country, part of the kingdom's Vision 2030 plan to diversify the economy from oil and attract international investment.

Air traffic in Saudi Arabia had been increasing rapidly. Scheduled growth in airplane seats in the market is up more than 23% this year from 2023, though the rise has recently slowed, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.

Whether travelers come back to the region depends on risk appetite. Ukassova said energy companies, which can depend on in-person visits to large projects, tend to have higher risk tolerance, while academics have a low bar for potential risks.

The conflicts have cut off big parts of airspace in the Middle East, mainly overIran. The outbreak of the Iran war in February set off massive aviation, travel and safety crises.

For example,Australian carrier Qantashas changed its Perth, Australia-to-London route to avoid Iranian airspace. Because that flight is then longer, the carrier has added a stop in Singapore to refuel.

For four years, Western commercial passenger and cargo planes have already had to fly longer routes to avoidRussian airspace. Carriers started detouring away from Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Taking longer routes to avoid potentially dangerous airspace has been adding to airlines'fuel bills, which got even more expensive this year due to those same Middle East conflicts.

While much of the traffic to Dubai and Doha has rebounded from the first days of the war since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, it remains below 2025 levels, according to flight-data firm OAG. Capacity by seats across the Middle East is down 5.7% in October from last year, 2.2 million fewer seats, OAG reported.

Some airlines are opting to stay away from the region altogether.

"We will not fly to Dubai and Doha, and we need to wait until the situation gets settled," Finnair CEO Turkka Kuusisto told reporters last month in New York.

title: More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
content:
More Republicans are speaking out against PresidentDonald Trump's decision to letVladimir Putin's Russia temporarily export diesel fuel on the global market, expanding thebipartisan blowbackover the deal.

Six GOP senators joined six of their Democratic colleaguesin a letter Tuesdayurging Trump to cancel the arrangement allowing Russia to supply 4.8 million metric tons, or nearly 36 million barrels, of diesel through mid-April.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the lawmakers wrote.

Republican Sens.Thom Tillisof North Carolina,Susan Collinsof Maine, Oklahoma's Alan Armstrong,Lisa Murkowskiof Alaska, Kentucky'sMitch McConnellandJohn Cornynof Texas signed on, adding to the list of of GOP Congress members who had earlier questioned the deal Trump announced Friday. Armstrong has roots in the energy industry, having been CEO ofWilliams Companies, the largest natural gas-focused company in the U.S.

They joined Democratic Sens.Richard Blumenthalof Connecticut, New Hampshire'sJeanne Shaheen,Richard Durbinof Illinois, Delaware'sChris Coonsand Rhode Island'sSheldon WhitehouseandJack Reed.

The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the letter.

Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had already spoken out, joining astatementwith Democrats on Sunday that urged Trump not to "provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians."

Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah had also joined that statement.

Trump announced the Russia diesel deal after a call with Putin. The announcement quickly drew an unusually critical response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who counts on continued U.S. support for his military. Trump, in turn, slammed Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should get anew president.

Trump claimed in Friday's announcement that the deal will help quickly and sharply bring record-high diesel prices down. But oil analysts don't think the Russian supply will be nearly enough to make a meaningful impact on prices.

The 12 senators who signed Tuesday's letter to Trump agreed, writing that the deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans."

"Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans," the senators told Trump.

"It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea," they wrote.

The senators also alleged, as other critics already have, that the diesel deal contradicts the bipartisan Russian sanctions law that Trump signed into law a few weeks before announcing the deal, which required lifting existing sanctions on Russia.

"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," their letter read.

"Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," they wrote.

"Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world."

Trump hasdoubled down on his decision. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" he wrote onTruth Socialon Monday.

title: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI
content:
Appleon Tuesday announceda new home hub called HomeView.

Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13.

Tuesday's launch event is the second under new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000.

Apple also announcednew Apple TVand HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.

The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.

Apple said that HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music.

"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's chief marketer Greg Joswiak said in a statement.

Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users.

Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.

But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus.

Apple said on Tuesday that its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.

Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales but also helps further lock customers into its own ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house.

Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone.

Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as new boss Ternus hasreportedlypushed the company to release products faster.

Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and comes after a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable.

title: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms
content:
Iran is reportedly working to bolster its military capabilities in preparation for possible renewed U.S. attacks after the November midterm elections.

The Wall Street JournalreportedTuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East.

The Journal's report also said the Iranian regime is preparing its population for war by holding rallies, sending paramilitaries to read war stories to young children and advertising training in firing defensive missiles.

U.S. President Donald TrumpsaidThursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.

The Iranian and U.S. governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Journal report.

Meanwhile, a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis – a Yemeni militant group backed by Tehran – said it had intercepted a ballistic missile shot at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, on ⁠Monday, news agency Reutersreported.

The Houthis have been attacking the Saudi capital since last week, launching multiple strikes on energy facilities and airports. One airport attackresultedin multiple deaths, including a pilot working for Saudi carrier Saudia.

The closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been extended until Saturday.

On Monday, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administrationurgedairlines to exercise caution when flying above or near Saudi Arabia.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British lawmakers on Monday that an attempted attack on an air force base in England was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."

Ed Miliband, the U.K.'s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to stress that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil."

British policearrestedfive men on Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism offenses over an alleged threat to RAF Fairford in the west of England, a Royal Air Force base that the U.S. Air Force has used to strike Iranian missile sites.

Trump latersaidthe U.S. had moved all its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to "a threat."

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece at White House's request
content:
U.S. Ambassador to GreeceKimberly Guilfoylesaid Tuesday she would resign, shortly after new White House press secretaryKatie Zachariasaid Guilfoyle was being asked to leave her post.

"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," Guilfoyle said in an X post.

Guilfoyle also broadly denied "recent allegations" against her, apparently referring to multiple critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about her conduct before and after becoming an ambassador, which had prompted questions about her job security.

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," Guilfoyle said in the post. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

The Wall Street Journal did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Guilfoyle's post.

PresidentDonald Trumpsuggested later Tuesday morning that the reporting on Guilfoyle's conduct prompted the call for her resignation.

"She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters outside the White House before boarding Marine One.

The president also pushed back when a reporter noted that Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Trump's eldest son,Donald Trump Jr., was almost a member of his family.

"No, she wasn't a member of my family," Trump replied. "She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago, but she wasn't."

Hours earlier, Zacharia revealed that the White House had urged Guilfoyle to step down.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said while taking questions from reporters at the White House briefing room for the first time. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."

Trump had signaled Monday evening that Guilfoyle could be on the chopping block.

"Well, we're looking at it," Trump said at the White House when a reporter asked if he was weighing firing the ambassador.

"Yeah, we're not happy," he added.

An attorney for Guilfoyle did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Zacharia's remark.

Guilfoyle's yearlong tenure in Athens was rocked last month by the first of multiple Wall Street Journal articles on conduct that has raised alarms among ethics experts and former government officials.

ASept. 25article alleged Guilfoyle persistently promoted a Greek company and involved a lobbyist for a Greek construction firm in meetings with foreign officials.

Her attorney, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal in response to that article that Guilfoyle has "worked with companies across the energy sector" and has not been focused on one company.

According to anOct. 7report from the Journal, Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters in July 2025 to wire $100,000 to quietly pay down her American Express bill prior to her congressional hearing to become an ambassador.

Binnall told the newspaper that Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events prior to being nominated and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events." Binnall also disputed the authenticity of messages from Guilfoyle reported in the article, but declined to provide specifics, according to the Journal.

On Saturday, the Journalreportedthat Guilfoyle in January boasted of her close ties to wealthy Greek businessmen as she sought an invite to a dinner being held for Eric Trump, another of the president's sons.

title: Paul Tudor Jones says 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market
content:
Legendary hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech initial public offerings coming down the pipe as well as a potential reckoning from the ballooning U.S. fiscal deficit.

"2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," Jones told "Squawk Box" on Tuesday. "You've probably got the most negative flow picture for the U.S. stock market that we've had, say, since 2002."

The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, have been a tail wind for the stock market for most of this four-year bull market as they decreased the equity supply.

That tide is now turning against the market with major offerings ahead in the AI space from Anthropic and OpenAI, along with one just finished forSpaceX. There will also likely be more secondary offerings from companies in order to raise money for the AI build-out, said Jones. It all adds up to an increased equity supply picture that could weight on prices.

The billionaire hedge fund manager's comments come as investors worry that a bull marketnow in its fourth yearcould start to dwindle and run out of steam as concerns grow around mounting inflation, higher bond yields and a more hawkish Federal Reserve.

Jones repeated that the current period in the market isakin to 1999, just about a year before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000. He noted the bifurcation in the current market between those companies benefiting from the AI boom and those that aren't.

He also added that a ballooning fiscal deficit is among the dangers for the current stock market, for which he thinks there could be a reckoning.

"We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. No politician is going to voluntarily raise taxes or cut spending. They're going to be forced to," he said.

"And the only question is, are we now at that tipping point where the market's about to do that? And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path," Jones said.

Oil, which he is long, is another headwind for the market, according to the hedge fund manager. Hecontended that prices could rally another $20 to $25 after the midterms, a scenario that the stock market will "hate" if it comes to pass.

"I'll be short the whole year. There just — there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in '98 and '99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."

title: Anthropic to disclose new revenue numbers as AI lab financials become central to tech trade
content:
Anthropicplans to disclose its third-quarter financials for the first time at a meeting with potential investors on Wednesday as theartificial intelligencegiant prepares for what could be the largest initial public offering in history.

San Francisco-based Anthropic will release the numbers to a group of institutional investors, according to two people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential.

Bloombergfirst reported that the meeting was happening. Anthropic declined to comment.

The meeting comes as revenue numbers from the private AI giants have proven to have an outsized impact on broader markets.

Last week, confusion around a report detailingOpenAI's revenue and updated accounting dragged downmajor semiconductor stocksand the broader Nasdaq.

OpenAI shared an updated revenue number of $50 billion with current investors as part of anongoing fundraise, which was lower than the $70 billion that had been widely reported. The updated number stripped out revenue from cloud partners, and wasn't an indication of changing demand, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal information.

It's unclear if Anthropic will account for sales in the same manner and include partner revenue, but the numbers this week will give investors a more accurate snapshot of Anthropic's growth and profitability as they look to value the company ahead of an IPO. It will also help Anthropic senior executives and bankers gauge investor interest and weigh the reaction to these updated financials.

Anthropic is plowing ahead with what could be a $2 trillion listing based on its latest reported revenue numbers, which could top $100 billion by the end of this year, according to people familiar with the plans.

That valuation would put it ahead ofSpaceX's historic debut.

Anthropic filed confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this year but has not made its S-1 financials public. The company will list in November, according to Reuters, but people familiar with the plans could not confirm a listing date. If it does go ahead, Anthropic will also be listing at a time when climbing interest rates are shaking parts of the AI trade.

Comments fromBroadcomCEO Hock Tan this week further rattled AI names. Tan said at a conference on Monday that with rates climbing, access to capital could be the biggest constraint on AI companies.

Chip stocks were lower Tuesday, extending an overnight sell-off sparked by worries over the durability of AI financing.

Market conditions are one of the biggest factors in Anthropic's upcoming IPO, and bankers are closely watching investor appetite for growth and AI stocks.

title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterPublished4 hours agoCountries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF).What the IMF says matters â it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world.Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel.Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report.1. The UK is weathering the Iran war better than expectedThe global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran.The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise.To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months.Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI).And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true.2. The UK is doing better than other major economiesThere is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this.The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both.By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments."So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said.Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany.Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context."We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are."3. But things could get worseWhile the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year.While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest.In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%."There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot.He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year.Related topicsUK economyInflationEconomyInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)Economic growthCompaniesPersonal financeMore on this storyUK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next yearPublished6 hours agoWhat is the Budget and what could be in it?Published2 hours ago

title: BA flight forced to turn back over cracked window
content: Image source,Wirestock/Getty ImagesImage caption,File photo of a British Airways planeBySimon BrowningTransport producerPublished4 hours agoA British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window.Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick.AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert".A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey."We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said.Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft.Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off.The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet.And in August Serbian national Ljubisa KaroviÄ's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object.Additional reporting by Emily Coady-StempRelated topicsGatwick AirportAir travelTravelTransportMore on this story'If we die, we die together': Wife of man nearly sucked out of Ryanair plane speaks of ordealPublished14 JulyRyanair broken window may have been caused by 'foreign object'Published21 July

title: Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterPublished7 hours agoThe owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident.According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands"."We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement.Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group.TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate".The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident."As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said.The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly."We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added.Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers".Fashion giants ranging fromAdidastoAlexander McQueenhave been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom."No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages.Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once".She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become".H&M investigating hack claimOn Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters.The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacksincluding targeting the FBI, Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster."We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement."At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised."It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group,via a push notification appearing on their phone screens.Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note".It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customersthan the retailer initially suggested.An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK?
