title: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
content:
India's headlineinflation rose to 5.54%in September from4.82% in August, adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy.

The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September.

Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest ratesfor the first time since 2023, joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause.

India is among the countries mostvulnerable to the supply disruptionscaused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through theStrait of Hormuz.

Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias.

India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-termtarget of 4%.

The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity.

Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face anadded risk from the Super El Nino, with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs.

The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions.

HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

title: AI FOMO driving some family offices into tech investments, survey suggests
content:
A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer.Sign upto receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Eighty-five percent of family offices rank artificial intelligence as their top investment theme, despite 75% expecting an AI bubble to burst within the next five years, according to a new survey. The poll of 155 North American family offices was conducted by RBC Wealth Management and Campden Wealth.

RBC's Bill Ringham said these mixed feelings about AI can be traced to several potential factors, including cautious optimism about the technology and concerns about sitting on the sidelines of an investment boom.

"Even patient capital can be caught up in the fear of missing out," said the director of private wealth strategies.

A combined 85% of respondents ranked AI an asset class or investment theme likely to reward investors over the next 12 months, the next two to five years, or both. The next most popular picks were U.S. equities and direct investments, selected by 76% and 72% of respondents, respectively.

However, while AI was the top investment theme of 2026 at 59%, family offices said they were more bullish on U.S. equities in the long run. When asked about returns over the next two to five years, 69% of respondents chose U.S. equities compared to 64% for AI. Direct investments closely followed at 62%. And while only 26% of family offices said real estate was likely to reward shareholders over the next 12 months, nearly twice as many (51%) picked it as a rewarding investment in the two- to five-year horizon.

Ringham said the results may reflect how AI enthusiasm is influencing investors' short-term focus more than their long-term strategy.

"Fear of missing out is a short-term view," he said. "You're seeing AI over the next 12 months as being that top priority. Their long-term look swings back."

Ringham said family offices were cautiously optimistic about AI, especially in the startup space.

"Those optimists are also not afraid to say that there might be a bubble down the road," he said. "You're investing in what you think is going to be incredibly successful in the longer term. But at this stage, there are so many new companies that you really have to go into these things with your eyes wide open."

The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them.

Subscribe here to get access today.

The survey found that 76% of respondents ranked "excessive government borrowing" as the top market risk likely to crystallize over the next five years. That was followed by "AI investment bubble burst" (75%) and "AI advancements impact employment" (66%).

While the survey did not ask how family offices planned to change their allocations around AI, Ringham said that many asset classes are touched by the technology. 31% of family offices planned to make more direct investments in private equity and just over a fifth said the same of real estate and venture capital, respectively.

"I'm sure AI is embedded in a lot of those underlying categories," he said.

title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck
content:
SINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models.

"[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns.

"If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said.

Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity.

The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns.

Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands.

"[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now."

He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online.

Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure.

"There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030.

Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power.

But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said.

Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau.

Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

title: Why some have no choice but to pay costly oil prices
content: Image caption,Many heating oil customers are having to buy early in preparation for the colder monthsByMarie Lennon,ÂPolitical reporter, WiltshireÂandÂEdward Rowe,ÂPolitical reporter, GloucestershirePublished5 hours agoAs the temperature drops, some of us will start putting the heating on but for the one-and-a-half million people across the UK that are not on the mains gas network - and who are relying instead on heating oil - that decision may give them pause.The vast majority of those people live in rural locations.The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global pricequickly gets passed on to customers.Tensions in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine are two issues currently both affecting supply which is causing prices to rise.More from GloucestershireAuthor shares how books have 'magical way' of reaching you when strugglingPublished1 day agoAccessible playground to 'allow all children to play'Published19 hours ago'What terminal cancer has taught me about life'Published2 days agoUntil March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when thewar in Iranstarted in March, itjumped to a high of 134ppl.After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice.The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them.How much is heating oil?Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil."I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over Â£550," he said.Mason said that last year "it was about Â£300 to fill up - it is horrendous".He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus Â£50 but it has never been as high as it is today."It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs."I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings."Image caption,Most tanks hold 500 litres of oil and would cost about Â£550 to fill currentlyDylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire.The 51-year-old said he was currently paying more for fuel than he ever had in the three years of running his business.He said he had had to put the prices of his services up to offset the rise.At the start of the year he would pay between Â£120 and Â£130 for a full tank, he said, but that had now gone up to Â£160."It's ever increasing, ever worrying - keeping an eye on the news, keeping an eye on the diesel prices," he said."I mean I've got fuel cards... you don't pay the pump prices, you pay the fuel card prices but it doesn't make much a difference these days."It's a few pence really."Image caption,Tristan Holland (pictured with Mel Holland) runs a small team of community care workersYvette Farrell, volunteer director for Dean Forest Kitchen, which cook fresh meals every day and delivers them to clients within the Forest of Dean, said they might have to increase prices as there's "not going to be much choice in the future".She said: "It's impacted us a lot because we work on a not-for-profit scenario so there is not a lot of wiggle room when it comes to increase in any expenses."So the cost of fuel is really, really hitting the business hard and we're having to do our best to still keep going to our clients who are spread across a very rural area with no public transport."But we have to take these meals to them because... they will not have somebody coming to see them during the day because they're so isolated."Tristan Holland, company director at TLC Support Service, manages a small team of community care workers who travel around Wotton-under-Edge and Dursley.Staff use their own vehicles and the company pays mileage at 55p per business mile.He said: "We had an increase in our fees back at the start of the year, just kind of taking into account all the extras that were coming in this year but even that does make it tight."Everything has risen - the cost of the fuel, the training, even the uniforms that we purchased."Everything has gone up and so we try to keep our services as affordable as we possibly can but there has to be a profit or else we just can't carry on going."Will prices come down?The Iran war has disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and prices can rise or fall based on the words and actions of key political figures.It is thought prices could come down if there is a peace deal between the US and Iran.For people who rely on heating oil, it means feeling helpless.Richard Willan, who runs the Nadder Oil Buying Club in Wiltshire where more than 1,000 residents buy in bulk together to get a better price, said rural residents were increasingly vulnerable as the colder months set in."We are watching to see what happens with (Donald) Trump in the mid-term elections in America, that might change things again," he said.The Competitions and Markets Authority (CMA) said heating oil customers in remote areas were too vulnerable to price shocks.CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell said: "Stronger safeguards are needed - including regulatory oversight and better support for vulnerable consumers as well as communities living in areas of the UK that are particularly exposed to higher and more volatile prices."What help is available?As prices sit above 100ppl with the temperature falling, there are calls for more support for rural communities.Chief Executive of Action in Rural Communities England Corinne Pluchino said: "Without specific targeted support for heating oil and LPG users, thousands of rural people risk becoming the forgotten victims of the energy crisis."The organisation is asking the government to remove VAT on heating oil and LPG for six months in this month's budget.There are also locally-run support schemes like the Surviving Winter campaign run by a group of charities in Wiltshire which supported more than 3,000 people last year with the cost of heating.A spokesperson for the Department for the Environment and Net Zero said: "We are helping thousands of households on heating oil switch to clean heat with grants worth Â£9,000, alongside a dedicated resilience fund for areas with higher rates of oil heating."We urge eligible households to apply."Get in touchYour VoiceContact formFollow BBC Wiltshire onFacebook,external,X,externalandInstagram,external. Send your story ideas to us on email or viaWhatsApp on 0800 313 4630.Related topicsCost of LivingRural lifeOilGloucestershireMore on this storyFuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soarPublished4 days agoFuel prices leave people asking 'what can we do?'Published1 OctoberUK diesel prices top Â£2 a litre for first time, RAC saysPublished2 October

title: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads
content:
A federal judge inNew Yorkordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded televisionadsfeaturing PresidentDonald Trumpthat critics call political propaganda intended to influence the Novembermidterm election.

Thetemporary restraining orderby Judge Jennifer Rochon in Manhattan federal court also bars theDepartment of Homeland Securityfrom spending any more of the$20 millionallocated for the ad campaign. About $19 million of that allocation has already been spent on the ads.

The order came a day after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office, which is defending the Trump administration in a lawsuit challenging the ads, told Rochon that the ads would not continue being aired past Sunday.

Rochon's order, which lasts 14 days unless extended, directs the Trump administration to cancel all scheduled ads, including those due to air on Sunday evening. The ads have included the caption "Paid for by the U.S. Government" since they began being aired.

The Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office declined to comment. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The money for the ads came from a large appropriation by Congress for immigration enforcement.

The coalition of plaintiffs that sued to block the ads told Rochon earlier Sunday that she should issue the TRO despite the claim by the U.S. Attorney's Office that the ads would not continue past Sunday.

"Defendants admit that appropriated funds were used to pay for political ads and do not disputethat this use of taxpayer money is unlawful," the plaintiffs said in a court filing Sunday.

"Instead, much of Defendants' opposition boils down to a single premise: it is too late for the Court to act. That is not because Defendants have stopped airing the ads," the plaintiffs said. "Indeed, Defendants assert — boldly, given their failure to defend the ads on the merits — that ads will continue to air today, including during evening programming that will attract millions of viewers."

Rochon agreed, saying in her order that the TRO request was not rendered moot by the U.S. Attorney's statement that the ads would stop Sunday. The judge also rejected an argument by the Justice Department that the coalition lacked legal standing to challenge the ads.

Rochon said the coalition has shown it was likely to win the lawsuit, that it would suffer irreparable harm if the TRO was not granted, and that "an injunction serves the public interest."

In addition to the other actions, the judge ordered the Trump administration not to enter into any new agreement or expand existing ones for the ads. And she stayed a purchase order for the ads between U.S. Customs and Border Protection and a contractor, Lepugh Inc., doing business as LMD Agency Inc.

Rochon said she would soon issue a full opinion explaining her ruling.

The coalition, which filed its lawsuit on Oct. 7, includes the advocacy group Common Cause and the Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, which is headquartered in New York City.

A separate lawsuit challenging the ads was filed that same day by the Democratic National Committee.

The ads, which have been airing for weeks, drew criticism from Democrats who said they appear designed to help Trump's fellow Republicans in November's election, which will determine which political party controls both chambers of Congress.

In its lawsuit, the coalition described one ad, titled "The Country He Loves," as featuring "rapid cuts of photos and videos of President Trump mixed in with text touting what the President views as his accomplishments in office," which includes "Largest Tax Cuts in History;" "Reigniting American Manufacturing;" and "Defend Law and Order and Police."

"Between those messages, the screen repeatedly flashes the words "AMERICA WILL NEVER BE A COMMUNIST COUNTRY," the civil complaint noted.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., wrote White House chief of staff Susie Wiles on Sept. 24, a day after that ad first aired.

"The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates,'" Hassan wrote.

Trump, in the face of that criticism, on Oct. 5 said that going forward he or his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads. The White House later said the president would not reimburse the federal government for the cost of the ads that had already aired.

In a statement Sunday evening on Rochon's order, the coalition said, "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda."

"There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the coalition said, referring to President Donald Trump.

"As this case moves forward and voters make their voices heard in this election, we will work to ensure the rule of law continues to be upheld, protecting the rights of voters and our democracy."

title: Oil falls after Trump declares 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine
content:
Oil fell Monday on optimism of improved supplies after President Donald Trump said that Russia and Ukrainewill not be targetingeach other's energy facilities, while Iran reached out to Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks against the kingdom.

Futures for international benchmarkBrent crudefor December delivery dropped 1.65% to $102.99 a barrel. U.S.West Texas Intermediate futuresfor November declined 1.92% to $90.09 per barrel.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump said in a social media statement.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on social media that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well."

Prospects of more Russian energy hitting markets after a deal with the U.S. have also risen after Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under a deal he struck with Putin during a phone call.

According to theSaudi state news agency, Iran's Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi made a phone call to Saudi Arabia's Minister of Foreign Affairs Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah, to discuss about the region's recent escalation of events as well as the efforts to address it.

Al JazeerareportedAraghchi had said Iran was ready to provide assistance to help with the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis.

Oil prices are expected to remain volatile in the near term as the U.S.-Iran conflict continues, while the impact of Hurricane Isaias on U.S. energy producers could also hurt supplies .

"The pressure on oil prices could remain on the upside as Hurricane Isaias strengthened to Category 3 with 120mph winds as it approached the US Gulf Coast, forcing energy producers to curtail offshore output," UOB said in a note on Monday.

"Separately, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport on Sat which killed 12 people and injured over 300, have materially elevated Middle East risk premia," UOB added.

title: Why China is importing a record amount of gold — and what it means for prices
content:
China's central bank has bought gold for 23 straight months, and the country is importing more of the precious metal than ever.

That buying spree reflects Beijing's push to cut its dependence on the dollar, and Chinese households' lack of safe alternatives, with analysts expecting sustained demand for the bullion in a struggling economy.

The People's Bank of Chinaadded about 23 tonnesin September, itsbiggest monthly purchasein almost three years, according to State Administration of Foreign Exchange data, extending thelongest purchasing streak since at least 2015.

Chinese households and companies are turning to gold as a safe haven. The country spent a record $158.8 billion, importing more than 1,000 tonnes in the first eight months of 2026, customs data show. That exceeds the $96.5 billion and 886 tonnes imported in all of 2025.

Consumer gold imports in China hit a record in the first eight months of this year, according to Aakash Doshi, head of gold strategy at State Street Investment Management. The surging premiums in China's onshore prices indicate "stronger winter seasonal demand," Doshi said.

The accumulation of the metal comes as gold prices have fallen. Theypulled back more than 8% in Septemberto about $4,176 an ounce, after inJanuary hitting a record above $5,500.

Doshi forecasts gold prices to rise to $4,750 to $5,500 per troy ounce by the end of the first quarter in 2027, buoyed by robust demand.

The PBOC's main motive is political, according to Carsten Menke, an analyst at Julius Baer Group, pointing to "the weaponization of the U.S. dollar and the related desire to be less dependent on U.S. Treasuries as a reserve asset."

Western governments froze Russia's central bank assets after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, underscoring how foreign-held reserves can be restricted at times of geopolitical friction, while gold in a country's own vaults remains insulated.

China has offloaded holdings of Treasurys, which reached an 18-year low of $618 billion in July, according to U.S. Treasury data, as Beijing continued todiversify its foreign-exchange reserves.

Chinese demand is also being fueled by gold's reputation as a safe haven. Consumers in the country, nervous about the shaky economy, are loading up on gold jewelry, bars and coins.

Domestic investors have few alternatives with the real estate market, once the main store of household wealth, locked in a multiyear slump. The benchmark CSI 300 index is down around 8% this year, versus the S&P 500's 13% gain. Returns from bank deposits and bonds have declined amid tepid borrowing demand. China's one-year government bond yield fell to around 1.2%,against about 4.46% in the U.S.

"The opportunity cost of holding gold is also much lower in China than in many Western markets," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank.

Adding to the momentum of the unprecedented buying is Beijing's plan to build a deeper domestic gold market, prompting it to replenish inventories, said Menke. He estimated that the central bank bought around 190 tonnes this year by end-August, including 110 tonnes that were unreported.

China's demand for gold has helped bullion withstand pressures that would have caused a deeper fall in prices, as buoyant U.S. yields kept a lid on demand for the non-yielding precious metal. The price of gold usually goes down when interest rates go up.

"Chinese buying has become an important source of structural support for gold prices," Ewa Manthey, commodities strategist at ING Bank. Central banks buy for the long term and are far less sensitive to price than retail investors, Manthey added.

Echoing that view, Carsten pointed out that gold prices have stayed above their levels in summer, even though interest rate expectations and bond yields have risen more sharply. The Federal Reserve has indicated another interest rate hike on the cards for 2026.

The world's fifth-largest gold holder owned 2,387 tonnes as of August,according to the World Gold Council, less than a third of the that held by the U.S.

Any renewed confidence in China's property and equities could blunt demand for gold, as well as a weaker yuan that makes gold pricier at home or higher interest rates that make deposits more attractive, Hansen said.

The larger shift would come if central banks lost interest in diversifying reserves and geopolitical tensions eased, Hansen said, adding that "neither appears particularly imminent."

title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
content: Image source,Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterPublished39 minutes agoMilk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology its a threat to humanity.The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have allbacked the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated."Let's get started today," he said.He said firms need "emergency brakes" â often known in the industry as 'kill switches' â to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology."We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of itsAI Security Institute,external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute."In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."'The moment has arrived'Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU."In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels â that's a strength," he said."When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived."Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."Figure caption,Microsoft President: Britain Should Write World's AI RulesAt the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House wherethe executives signed a "morally binding" document.The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways".Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it"."It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer."He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want"."It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about."Related topicsArtificial intelligenceMicrosoftCompanies

title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
content: Image source,Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesByDharshini David,ÂDeputy economics editorÂandÂTom Espiner,ÂBusiness reporterPublished43 minutes agoThe price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home."But Britain and our alliesâ¯can face up to these challenges together."He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring."A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said."Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course."Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.'Breathing space'Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around Â£10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around Â£20bn. That is less than the Â£24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra Â£25bn in 2029-30.That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.Related topicsUK economyInstitute for Fiscal StudiesJohn HealeyMore on this storyWhat is the Budget and what could be in it?Published3 days ago

title: Justice Department investigates TV networks as White House press-access fight escalates
content:
The U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation into whether the White House television press pool's decision to suspend coverage of PresidentDonald Trumpviolated antitrust laws.

The Justice Department said in a statement that it is examining whether theWhite House TV press pool— a group of broadcasters including CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC — violated the Sherman Act by temporarily halting pooled TV coverage of Trump.

The Sherman Act is a federal law that prohibits certain agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Introduced in the 1890s, the law has rarely been applied to media organizations, particularly regarding their coverage.

Members of the press pool did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment sent outside of normal business hours.

The DOJ investigation follows the White House television press poolceased its coverageof Trump on Sept. 21, shortly after he prohibited CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House.

In aTruth Social post, the president said then that those outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."

A judgelifted restrictionson those reporters on Sept. 24, several days after White House staff confiscated their press passes. Despite the ruling, reporters from CNN and Politico were barred from traveling with the president on Air Force One, the New York Timesreported.

The Trump administration nowfaces a lawsuit from CNN, MS NOW and Politicoover its ban of their reporters from the White House grounds.

Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed.

The DOJ investigation marks another escalation in an ongoing dispute between Trump and the media over press rights.

The Trump administration has moved to restrict news agencies that have produced critical coverage of its policies.

Last year, Trump moved to rescind about $1.1 billion previously approved for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, federal funding earmarked for public broadcasters NPR and PBS. Trump and his allies have also sued several media organizations, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and BBC News, over alleged biases or inaccuracies in their reporting.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, called the DOJ investigation "nonsense."

"Depriving Trump of the attention he craves is not a competitive harm and in any case, antitrust law has long recognized First Amendment exceptions even when there is anticompetitive impact," he said. "After all his 'fake news' rhetoric, Trump is weaponizing the DOJ to pressure the networks he calls the 'enemy of the people' to stay at the White House. It's a weird way of telling the press how much he missed them."

The White House Correspondents' Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

title: Trump declares 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine; Zelenskyy is waiting for details
content:
PresidentDonald TrumpclaimedRussiaandUkrainehad agreed to an "energy ceasefire" as the countries trade blows on energy infrastructure, but it's unclear whether either side has agreed to a truce.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump said in a social media statement, without providing details about the alleged pact.

The White House referred CNBC to the social media post when asked for more information on the ceasefire.

Trump's statement onTruth Socialcomes as energy costs soar globally during the U.S. war with Iran. An energy truce between Ukraine and Russia could help to alleviate the oil and gas crunch ahead of winter.

In a social media post, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said: "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well."

"We are awaiting details from the American side," Zelenskyy said. "For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace."

Earlier in the week, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy, suggesting he should be replaced andblaming himfor high diesel costs that threaten to complicate the Republican Party's chances ahead of November'smidterm election. Trump also said he had cut a deal with Russian PresidentVladimir Putinto bring Russian diesel to the market.

Zelenskyy said in response that Ukraine would only stop attacking oil refineries if Russia halted its attacks on Kyiv's electric grid.

Ceasefires between Russia and Ukraine have been consistently difficult to hold since Russia invaded its neighbor in 2022. Trump has repeatedly sought to end the conflict, but so far has been unsuccessful.

Zelenskyy onABC's "This Week"earlier Sunday asked Trump to "give them [a] signal, not [to] attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine."

"If they want energy ceasefire, we are open for this. Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attack[ing] your diesel," he said, according to a show transcript.

title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
content: Image source,ReutersImage caption,Yandex's data centres have been targeted three times this week - like this one in Sasovo on ThursdayByHafsa KhalilPublished11 October 2026, 13:50 BSTUpdated 1 hour agoYandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.Earlier this week,Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its servicesafter two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel dealPublished14 hours agoAnalysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel pricesPublished1 day agoYandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.Related topicsRussiaWar in UkraineMore on this storyNord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to UkrainePublished1 day agoRussian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and fleePublished2 days agoFear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacksPublished5 days ago

title: Trump says he is 'going to look at' joining Saudi Arabia in the fight against Iran-backed Houthis after deadly airport strike
content:
President Donald Trumpsaid he is considering joiningSaudi Arabiain its retaliation against Tehran-backedHouthisin Yemen after adeadly attackon Riyadh's main airport, a move that could draw the U.S. further into a second front in theIran war.

"We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday when asked if the U.S. would back Saudi Arabian strikes. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

Two Saudi Arabian government officials told MS NOW that the kingdom is requesting "urgent defense support" from the U.S. following the attacks.

The officials, including a senior member of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did not want to be identified because of the matter's sensitivity. They added that the U.S. needs to intervene "as soon as possible" to help the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen fight the Houthis.

The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the country's official Saudi Gazette media outletreported.

Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Houthis, described the attack as a "war crime."

"Therefore, the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law," Al-Maliki said in aposton X.

It was the second deadly assault on Riyadh's airport in less than a week.

Three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, were killed in attacks on the facility by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Thursday.

Following Saturday's attack, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airports.

"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using ⁠Saudi ‌airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become ⁠a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in aposton X.

Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the Middle East, intervened in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and its internationally recognized government after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014.

Last month, the Trump administration approved the potential $24.3 billion sale of nearly 50 F-35 warplanes toSaudi Arabiain what was seen as a major boost for the kingdom as it facesintensifying attacksfrom the Houthis. The sale is under congressional review.

The Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference will still take place in Riyadh on Sunday, Reuters reported.

The five-day WPC Energy Congress ⁠is taking place at a convention center near King Khalid airport. State television told Reuters that more than 70 ministers, ⁠300 company executives and representatives of more than 25 international energy organizations have confirmed their attendance, though it was not clear ⁠whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.

Reuters said a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to take place, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors.

In addition to attacks on civil aviation, the Houthis have also been trying to choke off oil tanker traffic through the Bab el Mandeb strait, a key entry point to the Red Sea, as Iran has effectively done in the Strait of Hormuz to the north of the Arabian Peninsula.

Earlier this month, Yemeni government forces said they reclaimed thestrategic port city of Mokhafrom the Houthis.

Energy prices have soared since the start of the Iran war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, putting pressure on consumers globally.

The surge in domestic fuel prices has been a key issue for voters ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.

But that support would be expensive militarily.

"Potential U.S. involvement in the Saudi-Yemeni government air campaign to degrade Houthi ballistic missile capabilities would mark the first direct U.S. military action against the group since the conclusion of Operation Rough Rider in May 2025," according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.

The offensive aimed to suppress the Houthis' capabilities, but recent attacks show the group has regrouped.

"After seven months of war, there are questions about the U.S. capacity to wage a sustained campaign against the Houthis, return to combat against Iran if necessary, and prepare for contingencies in other parts of the world, notably East Asia," Steven Cook, an expert on Arab and Turkish politics at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank,wrotelast month.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom's defense secretary said his government is also examining how to support Saudi Arabia.

"I've spoken to my Saudi counterpart [Khalid bin Salman] on a number of occasions in recent weeks to look at what more we can do to support Saudi Arabia, and I'm afraid last night explains precisely why we are providing that support," Wes Streeting said in an interview on BBC television on Sunday.

Streeting said the U.K. is not getting involved in offensive operations "at this stage."

"We've always been clear that there isn't a military solution to this conflict," Streeting added.

title: AI’s quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight
content:
Two months ago, independent evaluators occupied a relatively sleepy corner of the multitrillion-dollarartificial intelligenceindustry. Now they're being asked to come to its rescue.

WhileAnthropicandOpenAIare at the heart of a fierce debate over whether they can safeguard their advanced models and grow their businesses simultaneously, they're seeking support from a handful of small third-party groups like Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), Apollo Research, and Transluce.

The evaluators, which mostly operate as nonprofits, are still finding their footing in an industry where capital is flowing at historic levels and new models are rolling out faster than ever. Their primary role has been to assess AI model capabilities and risks and to flag instances where the technology behaves badly.

Without a federal push for regulation, evaluators have taken on outsized importance. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pledged to embed independent evaluators in his company last month – a move that OpenAI CEOSam Altmanquicklyendorsed. PresidentDonald Trumpsupported the idea, as did most of the largest U.S. tech companies. But left unanswered are questions about how those third parties should be funded, what level of access they will have and what the reporting structure will ultimately look like.

"To a degree, the problem, as always, is money," Suresh Venkatasubramanian, a computer science professor at Brown University, told CNBC in an interview. "Who is paying for these companies to do their work? How are they going to support them? You need an ecosystem, you need a viable business model for this."

Right now, Anthropic, OpenAI and the infrastructure partners that are profiting from the AI boom are writing the rules. Critics say that's likeaskingthe biggest banks to protect us from a financial crisis orallowingpharmaceutical companies to put drugs on the market without regulatory clearance.

Trump recentlylauded AI executivesfor their "tremendous self-policing," andsignaledthat he intends to leave companies to their own devices, unwilling to impede the growth of the industry that's driving the economy and stock market. The president encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented in late September.

Amodei kicked off the conversation in his viral essay last month, when hecalledfor a "slower pace" in advanced model development after researchers left his company and voiced concerns about the existential threats the technology poses.

As AI labs move to put evaluators in place, friction is already emerging.

OpenAI fired three employees last week for "violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," according to a spokesperson. Two of those employees, Mikita Balesni and Tomek Korbak, said they believe they were dismissed because of how they communicated with third-party evaluators.

"My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe," Balesni wrote ina post on Xon Thursday. "They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties. I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors."

OpenAI disputed that characterization and said in aposton Friday that it's "actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks."

"We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work," OpenAI wrote.

An OpenAI spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its upcoming work with evaluators "builds on existing collaboration with independent safety organizations," including METR and Redwood Research.

Anthropic didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment.

The AI evaluator ecosystem consists mostly of small organizations, including METR and Apollo Research, and larger accounting and auditing firms likeAccenture.

AI labs have worked with evaluators in limited capacities, but Andrew Freedman, CEO of policy nonprofit Fathom, said the field is maturing quickly.

"I've worked in politics and policy for the last 20 years of my life, and I've never seen an issue move so fast on so many different political spectrums," Freedman told CNBC in an interview. He said he expects an "influx of capital" to flow into the ecosystem.

Rayan Krishnan, CEO of independent evaluatorVals AI, said his for-profit startup, which builds benchmarks to measure how AI models perform on industry-specific tasks, has grown from eight employees to roughly 30 this year and announced a $40 million funding round in August.

METR, a nonprofit,announced in Augustthat it had raised commitments of around $71 million over the last six months. That's up from total 2024 contributions of $13.6 million, according to the group'smost recent filingwith the Internal Revenue Service.

By late that month, METR's profile had risen further. OpenAI enlisted two of its employees and a contractor to put together apostmortem reportdetailing how the company's modelsescaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached open-source developer platformHugging Face. METR said it did not accept payment from OpenAI for the assessment.

Kevin Werbach, faculty director of the Wharton Accountable AI Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said the ecosystem is "not robust enough right now." For example, METR employs fewer than 50 full-time staffers, according to its website.

The power imbalance between small evaluators and leading labs that have raised tens of billions of dollars and employ thousands of people raises questions about potential conflicts.

"If you want true third-party evaluation, you need true independence financially and otherwise," said Venkatasubramanian. "It's not just a matter of not getting paid, it's a matter of, will there be consequences if I am an auditor and I put out a report that looks unfavorable to this company? Is my business going to dry up?"

Anthropic acknowledged the complexity ina blog postlast month, announcing it willembed employeesfrom Faculty, Accenture's specialist AI business, to test safeguards and assess whether models will behave in line with human values. Anthropic said that "given the importance and urgency of this work," it will fund Accenture's contributions directly.

"There are, as yet, no standards for what information embedded evaluators should have access to, or how they should report what they find. There is also no settled system for funding independent evaluation," Anthropic said. "Long-term, we think funding should come from pooled or government sources."

Anthropic said it's in discussions with METR and other nonprofit evaluators that are planning to use their own funding to pilot "elements" of embedded evaluation.

InJuneof last year, Fathom introduced amarketplace frameworkfor Independent Verification Organizations, or IVOs. The government would license these groups and authorize them to test whether AI companies meet various safety criteria.

Freedman, the group's CEO, said government oversight is key because, without it, third-party evaluators could become beholden to large AI labs for revenue, incentivizing them to "start rubber-stamping stuff" to maintain favor.

IVOs are a key provision of the ''Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting" (FRONTIER)Act, which Reps. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., and Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., introduced in July. Freedman said Fathom helped draft language and provided technical expertise for the bill.

OpenAI global affairs chief Chris Lehane told reporters in September that he sat down with one of the bill's sponsors on Capitol Hill to express support for the IVO provision.

"It was important for them to hear that and hear it from us, and we wanted to be really clear about that," Lehane said,according to reports.

Meanwhile, lawmakers in California, Connecticut and Virginia have taken steps to implement IVOs, and states like Massachusetts are weighing independent safety evaluations more broadly.

California Governor Gavin Newsom recentlysigned two billsinvolving IVOs, one establishing a "first-in-the-nation framework," and the other creating a state registry for AI auditors. Anthropic threw itssupport behind both billsin August, and OpenAI formally endorsed them last month, the same day Newsom signed them into law.

Lehane wrote ina blog postat the time that "we prefer independent technical assessments to be required at the federal level," but in the absence of federal action, "California can help establish the rules of the road."

Freedman said he thinks it will be "really difficult" for companies like OpenAI and Anthropic to work out how to engage with independent evaluators on their own. However, with the government's role unclear, "it's a muscle worth developing in the interim," he said.

For now, the industry's closest thing to a set of standards is what Trump called a "morally binding" agreement at aluncheonhe hosted for tech leaders at the White House late last month.

Theone-page accordsays that "every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public." It also encourages signees to work with an "independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments."

title: Some in Florida and Alabama without power as Isaias moves north to Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic
content:
Nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power early Sunday as remnants of Isaias moved north, where widespread moderate to heavy rainfall was expected across the central Appalachians and mid-Atlantic region.

Heavy rainfall was expected to be the "primary hazard" as the storm moves north, said Philippe Papin, a senior hurricane specialist at the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Parts of the southeastern U.S. and mid-Atlantic could see scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts, according to the National Weather Service.

"We're expecting that heavy rainfall to continue here across the central Appalachians into the mid-Atlantic here during the day on Sunday, and we're still expecting isolated flash and urban flooding, and there may be also some residual gusty winds associated with the system as it continues to kind of move up the spine of the Appalachian mountains," Papin said.

At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.

Isaias made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops.

Despite warnings of storm surges, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak Saturday and free of the downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.

Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city's mayor said the airport "took some damage." The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of a high-rise facade in Panama City Beach.

A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building's insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about.

In Florida's Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home, and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man's family members, ranging in age from 4 to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said.

Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds.

One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city's fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state's emergency management agency.

Along Alabama's Gulf Coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after earlier doing the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid.

The U.S. Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation's strategic petroleum reserve to address storm-related supply disruptions.

The National Weather Service said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods.

Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon was a Category 4 storm with 150 mph (241 kph) winds as it approached Mexico's coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico beginning Sunday, with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Papin said Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California after becoming a post-tropical cyclone overnight.

title: AI is automating coding. So why are software developer job postings on the rise?
content:
U.S. software development job postings have risen since February 2025, the launch date for Anthropic's Claude Code, even asoverall job postingsfell, complicating predictions that AI would rapidly erase demand for developers.

Concerns about the future of the software development career are well-founded, and intensified as companies adopted AI-powered coding tools, especially as those tools keep getting better. As far back as 2023, Microsoft's software development platform GitHub said that on projects where AI was available, it was close to writing half of all code.

Some AI experts claim AI-written code across the entire GitHub platform has now passed thehalfway mark. GitHub has not confirmed that, but in October it did report that one in three "pull requests" — the process in which coders that collaborate on development propose code changes for projects — now involve an AI agent. A year ago, GitHub said that number was fewer than one in 10. "If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human,"it stated.

Labor market researchers say that against this backdrop, the profession is evolving rather than disappearing. Data from Indeed Hiring Lab shows that U.S. software-development job postings have risen nearly 15% since February 2025, bucking both the overall job market and the coding data.

Some economic experts are pointing to the rebound in software job postings as confirmation for a glass half-full view of AI and the job market. "It wasn't that long ago that we were reading the headline that there will be no more need for software developers," Eric Kutcher, North America chair at McKinsey, said during a recent interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Instead, he said, as companies are producing more code than ever before, software developers who work with AI remain in high demand. "We're seeing much more growth in the places we thought we were gonna see the biggest displacement," Kutcher said.

Recent researchon AI and the future of jobs from McKinsey Global Institute notes that the earlier decline in the software developer field was not solely an AI story. While in recent years AI has been automating software-development tasks, the rebound comes after a steep drop from a 2022 hiring peak, when technology companies pulled back after a pandemic-era surge in hiring.

But even after the recovery, software-development job postings remain about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level, according toIndeed Hiring Lab data. Importantly, the increase is concentrated in senior-level roles and more experienced AI-oriented positions. Indeed Hiring Lab found that senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software-development postings between May 2025 and May 2026. Job titles that mention AI accounted for 37% of the increase.

AI tools may be allowing companies to produce code more quickly than developers could on their own. GitHub leaders have said in the past that as much if not more than 80% of code could eventually be written by AI, especially as developers become more comfortable working with AI tools. But that also could mean the demand for workers is concentrated on those who can evaluate AI-generated code or problems and connect new tools to an organization's broader technology systems.

Sneha Puri, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said companies are realizing that even if AI can handle some technical coding tasks, they still need developers to oversee that work, refine products and help clients integrate the technology into their day to day operations. One example, she said, is the growing need for workers who can help businesses apply AI tools beyond simply building them.

Right now, factors like the ones cited by Puri are helping software developers to be among winners in the earliest stage of the AI transformation of the labor market. Arecent analysisof U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data from economist Steve Rattner found that software developer was among the career categories that showed positive growth from May 2023 to May 2025, though it was merely in line with growth across all occupation and well below the pace of growth in traditionallyblue-collar jobsassociated with building AI data centers.

Anthropic researchersfound that even with automation, humans are still needed to oversee that automation and require user input. But the researchers cautioned that it is "by no means certain that this pattern will persist into the future."

GitHub said in its report on pull requests that the as AI pushed more code into the world, and with it, more risks in the code, humans must be in a position to scale with the technology to police the AI's work. But that may not be possible forever. "As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce the human effort required by those that remain, or else the volume of vulnerabilities introduced will become untenable," it wrote.

For the youngest workers, the software development field outlook remains uncertain. Stanford University's 2026 AI index found thatemploymentin AI-exposed fields for those aged 22 to 25 has fallen 16% since the rise of generative AI, with those identified as early-career software developers seeing a larger decline in employment of 20% as older developer roles expand.

That shift has made the path into software development more difficult for recent graduates, even as demand rises for more experienced workers. Puri said students should build familiarity with AI tools but not neglect the skills that remain central when working with them. "Being able to use AI in your work and improve your efficiency is a great place to start," Puri said. "But communication, interpersonal skills and leadership are also really important," she added.

Puri said employers also have a role to play in preserving routes into the field. "Today's entry-level talent becomes tomorrow's senior experts," she said. "If employers don't build those pipelines now, they're not going to have senior talent they need 10 years down the line."

While forecasting job growth in the AI era is difficult, the long-term outlook for software developers remains positive, according toan August reportfrom the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. It projects employment of software developers will grow 10% from 2025 to 2035, increasing from about 1.72 million to 1.89 million jobs and adding roughly 174,700 positions.

title: I’m a psychologist who studies couples: The No. 1 way to end a fight before it escalates—it works ‘almost immediately’
content:
Couples tend to slide off-course when they argue.

You might start out talking about something real and specific. Maybe a plan that was altered without a check-in or an impulse purchase that should have been discussed. Then suddenly you've stopped talking about that thing and started talking about each other:

One minute you're trying to solve a problem together, and the next you're each trying to prove you're the more reasonable person in the room. And once an argument becomes about that, it can't really be resolved. Because now, the battlefield and ammunition are endless.

As a psychologist who studies couples, I know that, thankfully, there's a practice that can act as a guardrail for disagreements. I call it a partial yield, and it prevents this all-too-familiar detour.

A partial yield is a type of phrase you use when you concede the specific piece of the argument you're genuinely responsible for, the moment it comes up, without conceding the rest of your position. It usually sounds very ordinary:

So you're not agreeing that you were wrong about everything. But you are admitting the fault that's actually yours, before your partner has to pry it out of you.

In my experience, nothing de-escalates a conflict faster.

When your partner confronts you, some part of them is preemptively braced for the effort of convincing you. It's why voices get louder and why examples start piling up. They're not trying to hurt you. They're trying to get you to believe them, and they've assumed it's going to be hard.

A partial yield releases the pent-up steam that can otherwise fuel an escalation. The effect is palpable almost immediately, and it rarely feels like a defeat for either person. Your partner gets the acknowledgment they were pushing for, and you get to be honest about your part without signing away the rest.

It's also easier on you than a full apology, which matters more than you might think. Most of us don't withhold small admissions because we believe we did nothing wrong. We withhold them because admitting to one thing feels like admitting to all the rest, too, and we'd rather concede nothing than concede everything.

I'd pay attention to what happens when you don't use a partial yield phrase.

If you never take accountability in the moment, the problem doesn't just go away. Your partner notices and files it away. They might bring it up again three weeks from now in the middle of an unrelated argument. It may look like score-keeping, but more often it's an old grievance that never got heard and owned, finally finding an opening.

Couples who concede small things routinely don't build up much of that "back-pocket" inventory, so there's nothing to reach for at a moment's notice. Their arguments tend to stay roughly within the context of whatever caused them.

A few steps differentiate a real partial yield from a fake one:

In my experience, genuine partial yields are the difference between couples who argue about — and solve — problems and couples who get stuck arguing about each other.

Mark Travers, Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist atAwake Therapy, a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness websiteTherapytips.org.
